reading.writerFeedback:
The engagement section is the strongest part of the draft and does the real work of the memo. The comparative numbers on session length, the retention figure, and the pinning frequency give the reader something concrete to hold onto, and the demographic observation lands well because you connect it directly to a monetization thesis in categories like home decor, fashion, and weddings. The risk section is admirably blunt and I would keep its brevity.

The weak spot is the summary line, which claims 'a defensible consumer position' when the body of the memo explicitly says the opposite - 'Defensibility against well-funded competitive responses is uncertain.' Those two sentences cannot both stand, and a reader on the IC will notice. I would also push you to say more about why diligence on Mr. Silbermann was 'deeply positive' beyond the Google reputation point, because right now the founder paragraph is the thinnest part of an otherwise disciplined write-up. Finally, given there is no revenue and no monetization plan, a sentence on what the next 12-18 months need to prove before the Series B would strengthen the close.

sentences.text: We are writing to inform you of a new investment in Pinterest (the "Company"), a visual discovery and bookmarking platform that lets users organize images they find interesting onto themed boards.

occurrences.extract: Re:        Pinterest — Series A

We seek partnership approval for a Series A investment of USD 10mm in Pinterest, Inc., a visual discovery and bookmarking platform, at a USD 40mm pre-money valuation. We would own approximately 20% on a fully-diluted basis.

Pinterest is a young company. The product has been in market for roughly 16 months. The team is small — six full-time employees plus the two founders. Revenue is currently zero; the founders are deferring monetisation in favour of continued growth in user engagement and product depth. By conventional venture metrics this is an early-stage bet.

Pinterest is a visual discovery tool. Users create themed boards onto which they "pin" images they want to remember, organise, or return to. Boards are organised by topic — recipes, home decor projects, fashion, weddings, gardening, and so on. Other users can follow specific boards or specific users, repin content, and discover content through curated category pages.

The mechanic sounds simple but the product has unusual characteristics. Most social products are conversation-focused; users post, others respond, and the engagement is fundamentally about communication between people. Pinterest is different. Users come to the site primarily to discover and organise — engagement is fundamentally with the content rather than with other people. This makes the engagement model unusually robust to network dynamics. A user can have meaningful, repeat engagement with Pinterest even with very few followers.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The engagement section is the strongest part of the draft and does the real work of the memo. The comparative numbers on session length, the retention figure, and the pinning frequency give the reader something concrete to hold onto, and the demographic observation lands well because you connect it directly to a monetization thesis in categories like home decor, fashion, and weddings. The risk section is admirably blunt and I would keep its brevity.

The weak spot is the summary line, which claims 'a defensible consumer position' when the body of the memo explicitly says the opposite - 'Defensibility against well-funded competitive responses is uncertain.' Those two sentences cannot both stand, and a reader on the IC will notice. I would also push you to say more about why diligence on Mr. Silbermann was 'deeply positive' beyond the Google reputation point, because right now the founder paragraph is the thinnest part of an otherwise disciplined write-up. Finally, given there is no revenue and no monetization plan, a sentence on what the next 12-18 months need to prove before the Series B would strengthen the close.

reading.writerFeedback:
Solid announcement overall - the strategic rationale lands clearly, and the detail on the composite layup investment during Westhaven's hold gives the reader a concrete sense of what changed under the prior owner. The forward-looking line on space applications is a nice close because it points to where Halden sees the upside without overpromising.

Two things to tighten. The revenue growth stat is undercooked - "grown at a compound annual rate of approximately 11 percent over the past five years" needs a % symbol and, more importantly, we should say grown from what to what, or at least name the end-year revenue, otherwise the number floats. Second, the customer description is vague: "supplies the major commercial aircraft original equipment manufacturers and the leading US defense primes" would be stronger with a named anchor customer or two, or at minimum a sense of concentration. Also worth adding a line on deal size or financing if we are cleared to disclose - right now a reader has no sense of scale.

reading.writerFeedback:
The Cirrus section is the strongest part of the draft - the growth story is told cleanly, the margin expansion is quantified, and the forward view follows naturally from the numbers. The ESG paragraph also lands well because each claim is backed by a concrete figure and a year-on-year comparison, which is what readers want in this section. The structure of moving from winner to laggard to portfolio-wide themes is sensible and easy to follow.

The Moreno passage is where I would push back. Saying the business is "fundamentally sound" while also extending the hold by two years reads as defensive, and the draft never quite explains what went wrong - we get the remediation (new CCO, new Chairman) before we get a diagnosis. I would also want a line on what the extended hold means for expected returns, because at the moment "we continue to view the underlying business as fundamentally sound" is doing a lot of work without much underneath it. One more thing worth considering: twelve SBTi commitments with eight approved is a good data point, but we should say what the denominator is, otherwise the reader cannot judge whether that is most of the portfolio or a small slice.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The Cirrus section is the strongest part of the draft - the growth story is told cleanly, the margin expansion is quantified, and the forward view follows naturally from the numbers. The ESG paragraph also lands well because each claim is backed by a concrete figure and a year-on-year comparison, which is what readers want in this section. The structure of moving from winner to laggard to portfolio-wide themes is sensible and easy to follow.

The Moreno passage is where I would push back. Saying the business is "fundamentally sound" while also extending the hold by two years reads as defensive, and the draft never quite explains what went wrong - we get the remediation (new CCO, new Chairman) before we get a diagnosis. I would also want a line on what the extended hold means for expected returns, because at the moment "we continue to view the underlying business as fundamentally sound" is doing a lot of work without much underneath it. One more thing worth considering: twelve SBTi commitments with eight approved is a good data point, but we should say what the denominator is, otherwise the reader cannot judge whether that is most of the portfolio or a small slice.

reading.writerFeedback:
The thesis lands with real clarity and the three-part test for which workflows get hit is the strongest thing here - it gives readers something concrete to apply rather than a vibe about agents. The disclaimer that "This is not a thesis about general intelligence" is well placed and will save you a lot of pointless arguments with readers who want to relitigate AGI timelines. The closing move to 15 investments grounds the piece and signals conviction without overselling.

Where it's weak is the middle. The sentence listing "financial services, healthcare administration, logistics, legal services, and accounting" is doing enormous work for one line and lands as a gesture rather than an argument - pick one and show the workflow, or cut the breadth claim. The predictions paragraph is similarly abstract: "deep changes to commercial models" and "winner-takes-most dynamics" are the two most interesting claims in the whole piece and they go by in a half-sentence each. I'd push you to either expand those into their own beats or drop them so the piece ends on the investment count rather than on handwaving. Also worth asking whether the verification characteristic needs an example - it's the least intuitive of the three and a reader could easily nod past it without understanding why it matters.

sentences.text: We believe the dominant pattern of the next decade will be vertical AI agents — software that doesn't just present a workflow for a human to complete, but completes the workflow itself, with the human stepping in only for exceptions, oversight, and high-stakes calls.

occurrences.extract: Why we believe the next decade of software belongs to vertical-AI agents

The combination of frontier large language models, mature agent frameworks, and an installed base of digitised business processes is creating the conditions for a new category of software: vertical AI agents. These are software systems that do not present a workflow for a human to complete, but rather complete the workflow themselves, with the human stepping in only for exception handling, oversight, and high-stakes decisions.

We have spent the past eighteen months meeting with founders, customers, and operators across a range of verticals to understand where vertical AI agents are most likely to take hold first. Our conclusions are summarised below.

Vertical AI agents will succeed first in workflows with three characteristics. First, the workflow must be high-volume and currently labour-intensive — meaning the economic value of replacing the workflow with an agent is meaningful and the current state involves significant human time. Second, the workflow must be largely deterministic at the level of individual decisions, with the complexity coming from volume rather than from one-off judgement calls. Third, the workflow must produce outputs that can be verified ex post — meaning the agent's work can be checked for quality without re-doing the work.

These three characteristics describe a meaningful share of back-office work in industries such as financial services, healthcare administration, logistics, legal services, and accounting. We expect vertical AI agents to displace meaningful portions of human work in these industries over the next five years. This is not a prediction about general intelligence — it is a prediction about the specific economic deployment of current and near-future AI capability.

We expect vertical-specific defensibility to be the principal source of competitive moat. General-purpose AI capabilities are increasingly available to all builders. What distinguishes one agent from another, particularly in regulated or domain-specific verticals, is depth of vertical knowledge, integration with vertical-specific data sources and systems, and trust earned through track record. We expect to see strong winner-takes-most dynamics in specific verticals, with the leading agent in each category establishing a sustainable advantage through accumulation of training data, customer trust, and integration depth.

We do not expect agents to replace all software. Many workflows do not fit the three characteristics above. Software for human use will remain enormously important — particularly in workflows that involve creative work, complex stakeholder management, or genuine judgement calls. The point is not that all software becomes agents; it is that an entire new category of software becomes possible alongside what already exists.

We are actively investing behind this thesis. Quanta Ventures has made fifteen investments in the agent category over the past two years, with a particular focus on regulated verticals where the combination of high-value workflows, deep domain requirements, and meaningful regulatory constraint creates the conditions for sustainable competitive moats.

sentences.text: We expect significant disruption to the incumbent vertical SaaS industry, deep changes to commercial models, and strong winner-takes-most dynamics emerging within each vertical category.

occurrences.extract: For the last fifteen years, the software industry has been organised around a relatively stable architectural pattern. SaaS companies have built workflows for specific user roles, deployed them to enterprise customers, and competed on user experience, integration depth, and feature breadth. The pattern has been enormously successful — it built Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, Atlassian, and a generation of multi-billion-dollar vertical SaaS platforms.

We expect a meaningful share of new vertical SaaS company formation to be agent-first rather than workflow-first. We are already seeing this in early-stage pipeline. Where a traditional vertical SaaS company would have built a product for a human to use, a new generation of companies is building agents that perform the work the human would have done, with a thinner human-facing interface focused on oversight and exception handling.

We expect significant disruption to the incumbent vertical SaaS industry. Incumbents have built defensible positions around workflow ownership, but those workflows are precisely what agents are positioned to replace. We expect incumbents to invest aggressively in their own agent capabilities — but we are sceptical that retrofitting agents onto products designed around human workflows will produce competitive outcomes. The architectural differences are too significant.

We expect deep changes to the buyer journey and to commercial models. Workflow-first SaaS is bought per-seat by line-of-business buyers. Agent-first software is bought based on tasks completed, decisions made, or outcomes delivered — and is bought by executives interested in operating leverage rather than by managers interested in productivity tools. The commercial conversations look different, the procurement processes look different, and the success metrics look different.

facts.extract: For the last fifteen years, the software industry has been organised around a relatively stable architectural pattern. SaaS companies have built workflows for specific user roles, deployed them to enterprise customers, and competed on user experience, integration depth, and feature breadth. The pattern has been enormously successful — it built Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, Atlassian, and a generation of multi-billion-dollar vertical SaaS platforms.

We expect significant disruption to the incumbent vertical SaaS industry. Incumbents have built defensible positions around workflow ownership, but those workflows are precisely what agents are positioned to replace. fixtures.writerFeedback:
The thesis lands with real clarity and the three-part test for which workflows get hit is the strongest thing here - it gives readers something concrete to apply rather than a vibe about agents. The disclaimer that "This is not a thesis about general intelligence" is well placed and will save you a lot of pointless arguments with readers who want to relitigate AGI timelines. The closing move to 15 investments grounds the piece and signals conviction without overselling.

Where it's weak is the middle. The sentence listing "financial services, healthcare administration, logistics, legal services, and accounting" is doing enormous work for one line and lands as a gesture rather than an argument - pick one and show the workflow, or cut the breadth claim. The predictions paragraph is similarly abstract: "deep changes to commercial models" and "winner-takes-most dynamics" are the two most interesting claims in the whole piece and they go by in a half-sentence each. I'd push you to either expand those into their own beats or drop them so the piece ends on the investment count rather than on handwaving. Also worth asking whether the verification characteristic needs an example - it's the least intuitive of the three and a reader could easily nod past it without understanding why it matters.

reading.writerFeedback:
The deal thesis comes through clearly and the structure works well. The competitive position is grounded in something concrete and verifiable - the point that the Company is one of three qualified suppliers for FDA Class II and MDR hip and knee components, with 18 to 24 month qualification cycles, does the heavy lifting that an LP memo of this kind needs. The growth and margin history is presented cleanly, and the four-pillar value creation plan is specific enough to be useful rather than generic, particularly the M&A section where you name a bounded target universe and an EV range.

The weaker stretch is the risk paragraph. Writing that semiconductor cyclicality, customer concentration, FX, and the founder transition are 'each is understood and reflected in our planning, with specific mitigations in place' tells the reader nothing and will stand out precisely because the rest of the memo is specific. I would give each risk a sentence, even a short one, especially the founder transition given the Schiller family is retaining 22%. I would also tighten the bridge between the pillars and the returns - the pillars imply margin uplift of 300-400 bps plus 9% revenue growth plus M&A, and it is not obvious how that reconciles to 2.4x and 19%, so a reader doing the arithmetic may come away unsure whether the base case is conservative or stretched. One more thing worth a look: the 'International margin expansion' label on the first pillar reads oddly when the substance is Swiss footprint consolidation and procurement, which are not really international levers.

sentences.text: We are writing to inform you of a new investment in Helvetia Precision Components (the "Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Alpine — Proposed acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG

We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC was founded in 1962 by Werner Schiller in Winterthur. The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

HPC has grown revenue from EUR 312 million in 2020 to EUR 587 million in 2024, a compound annual growth rate of 17.1%. EBITDA over the same period has expanded from EUR 48 million to EUR 103 million, with margins improving from 15.4% to 17.5%. Growth has been split roughly evenly between organic share gains and the contribution from the Indianapolis acquisition. Free cash flow conversion has averaged 71% across the period.
We are attracted to HPC for four reasons.

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

Second, the end markets HPC serves are structurally attractive. The orthopaedic implants market is forecast to grow at 5–6% annually through 2030, driven by ageing demographics in Europe and the United States. Aerospace component demand is recovering strongly post-COVID, with Airbus and Boeing collectively targeting build-rate increases of approximately 40% over the next five years. Semiconductor capital equipment demand is more cyclical, but HPC's exposure is weighted toward EUV-related components, where structural demand growth is robust.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. We are comfortable with this exposure given (a) the structural growth in EUV, and (b) HPC's flexible cost base, which allowed the Company to maintain EBITDA margins above 15% throughout the 2023 downturn.

Customer concentration is a watch item. HPC's largest customer, a global orthopaedic implants manufacturer, accounted for 18% of revenue in 2024. While the relationship is multi-decade and contractually backed by long-term supply agreements, any meaningful disruption to this account would materially impact Company performance.

Foreign exchange exposure is significant. Approximately 55% of revenue is denominated in EUR, 30% in USD, and the remainder in CHF and other currencies. Cost base is more heavily CHF-weighted given the Swiss manufacturing footprint. CHF strength against EUR over the past three years has cost HPC roughly 180 basis points of cumulative margin. We expect to hedge transaction exposure systematically post-close and have factored a normalised CHF/EUR rate of 0.98 into our base case.

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 11.0x EBITDA, marginally below the entry multiple, reflecting prudence regarding sector multiples five years forward. In our upside case, multiple expansion to 12.5x reflects the higher-margin, more diversified, larger-scale platform we expect HPC to become.

Petra Köhler, age 49, will become CEO upon close. She joined HPC in 2009 from Sulzer, where she ran the rotating equipment business. She has held the COO role at HPC since 2018 and is credited internally with the success of the Indianapolis integration. Reference checks across customers, suppliers, and former colleagues have been uniformly positive.

The CFO, Markus Zehnder, has been with HPC for 11 years and is well-regarded. We see no need to change this role. We will recruit a Chief Commercial Officer post-close — a role HPC has historically not had — to coordinate the global customer interface across the three end markets. We have already identified a strong candidate currently working in a senior commercial role at GF Machining Solutions.

HPC represents an attractive opportunity to acquire a category leader in a structurally growing market with a clear operational improvement plan and proven through-cycle resilience. The base case returns of 2.4x / 19% are in line with our private equity portfolio benchmarks, and we see meaningful upside optionality from M&A and end-market acceleration. The risks are well-understood and manageable. We recommend approval.

While the relationship is multi-decade and contractually backed by long-term supply agreements, any meaningful disruption to this account would materially impact Company performance.

Founder transition risk is moderate. Andreas Schiller, son of the founder, has served as CEO for 17 years and will step back to the board post-close. The Company has identified an internal successor — Petra Köhler, currently COO — who is well-regarded by the management team and customers. We have completed extensive reference checks. Andreas Schiller has committed to remain on the board for the first three years post-close and will rollover approximately 8% of his proceeds into the transaction.

The broader management team is mature, but we have identified the procurement function as under-resourced relative to the Company's scale and complexity. A Chief Procurement Officer will be recruited in year one, with a mandate to deliver the EUR 8–12 million of annualised procurement savings identified in diligence.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

Diligence has been thorough. We engaged Bain & Company on commercial diligence (six weeks, completed late February), Deloitte on financial and tax diligence, Kirkland & Ellis on legal, and ERM on ESG and environmental diligence. The Bain report — circulated separately — confirms our market positioning thesis and identifies an additional EUR 14 million of revenue synergies from cross-selling between segments that we have not underwritten in the base case.

occurrences.extract: We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC was founded in 1962 by Werner Schiller in Winterthur. The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

The Company operates four manufacturing facilities: a headquarters site in Winterthur (Switzerland), a larger production facility in Olten (Switzerland), a US operation in Indianapolis acquired in 2018, and a smaller Czech facility in Brno established in 2021 to serve European aerospace customers at lower cost. Total headcount stands at 1,420 employees, of whom approximately 240 are based outside Switzerland.

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. We are comfortable with this exposure given (a) the structural growth in EUV, and (b) HPC's flexible cost base, which allowed the Company to maintain EBITDA margins above 15% throughout the 2023 downturn.

Customer concentration is a watch item. HPC's largest customer, a global orthopaedic implants manufacturer, accounted for 18% of revenue in 2024. While the relationship is multi-decade and contractually backed by long-term supply agreements, any meaningful disruption to this account would materially impact Company performance.

Founder transition risk is moderate. Andreas Schiller, son of the founder, has served as CEO for 17 years and will step back to the board post-close. The Company has identified an internal successor — Petra Köhler, currently COO — who is well-regarded by the management team and customers. We have completed extensive reference checks. Andreas Schiller has committed to remain on the board for the first three years post-close and will rollover approximately 8% of his proceeds into the transaction.

The broader management team is mature, but we have identified the procurement function as under-resourced relative to the Company's scale and complexity. A Chief Procurement Officer will be recruited in year one, with a mandate to deliver the EUR 8–12 million of annualised procurement savings identified in diligence.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

Diligence has been thorough. We engaged Bain & Company on commercial diligence (six weeks, completed late February), Deloitte on financial and tax diligence, Kirkland & Ellis on legal, and ERM on ESG and environmental diligence. The Bain report — circulated separately — confirms our market positioning thesis and identifies an additional EUR 14 million of revenue synergies from cross-selling between segments that we have not underwritten in the base case.

occurrences.extract: We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC has grown revenue from EUR 312 million in 2020 to EUR 587 million in 2024, a compound annual growth rate of 17.1%. EBITDA over the same period has expanded from EUR 48 million to EUR 103 million, with margins improving from 15.4% to 17.5%. Growth has been split roughly evenly between organic share gains and the contribution from the Indianapolis acquisition. Free cash flow conversion has averaged 71% across the period.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. We are comfortable with this exposure given (a) the structural growth in EUV, and (b) HPC's flexible cost base, which allowed the Company to maintain EBITDA margins above 15% throughout the 2023 downturn.

EBITDA margin expansion from 17.5% to 21.0% over the hold period, delivering EBITDA of approximately EUR 190 million by 2029. The margin lift is sourced from the footprint consolidation programme (approximately 120 bps), procurement initiatives (approximately 80 bps), automation investment in Brno (approximately 60 bps), and operating leverage on incremental revenue (approximately 60 bps).

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 11.0x EBITDA, marginally below the entry multiple, reflecting prudence regarding sector multiples five years forward. In our upside case, multiple expansion to 12.5x reflects the higher-margin, more diversified, larger-scale platform we expect HPC to become.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

occurrences.extract: HPC was founded in 1962 by Werner Schiller in Winterthur. The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

Second, the end markets HPC serves are structurally attractive. The orthopaedic implants market is forecast to grow at 5–6% annually through 2030, driven by ageing demographics in Europe and the United States. Aerospace component demand is recovering strongly post-COVID, with Airbus and Boeing collectively targeting build-rate increases of approximately 40% over the next five years. Semiconductor capital equipment demand is more cyclical, but HPC's exposure is weighted toward EUV-related components, where structural demand growth is robust.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

Fourth, we see meaningful M&A opportunity. The European precision machining sector remains highly fragmented, with the top 10 players accounting for less than 30% of the market. We have already identified five actionable targets in the EUR 30–80 million enterprise value range that would be accretive on both growth and margin grounds. The founding family has historically been reluctant to pursue M&A; under our ownership we expect to complete two to three add-on acquisitions over the holding period.
Our base case underwrites a five-year hold with the following value drivers.

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 11.0x EBITDA, marginally below the entry multiple, reflecting prudence regarding sector multiples five years forward. In our upside case, multiple expansion to 12.5x reflects the higher-margin, more diversified, larger-scale platform we expect HPC to become.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

The Schiller family will retain a 15% economic interest. Management will hold the remaining 7%. We have negotiated standard tag-along and drag-along rights, and a clear governance framework giving Halden Group majority board representation (3 of 5 seats).

occurrences.extract: INVESTMENT MEMORANDUM — STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL
To:        Global Investment Committee
From:      European Industrials Team — Stefan Brunner (Partner), Lena Hofmann (Member of Management), Tobias Reichmann (Senior Vice President)
Date:      14 March 2025
Subject:   Project Alpine — Proposed acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG
RECOMMENDATION

We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC was founded in 1962 by Werner Schiller in Winterthur. The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

The Company operates four manufacturing facilities: a headquarters site in Winterthur (Switzerland), a larger production facility in Olten (Switzerland), a US operation in Indianapolis acquired in 2018, and a smaller Czech facility in Brno established in 2021 to serve European aerospace customers at lower cost. Total headcount stands at 1,420 employees, of whom approximately 240 are based outside Switzerland.

HPC has grown revenue from EUR 312 million in 2020 to EUR 587 million in 2024, a compound annual growth rate of 17.1%. EBITDA over the same period has expanded from EUR 48 million to EUR 103 million, with margins improving from 15.4% to 17.5%. Growth has been split roughly evenly between organic share gains and the contribution from the Indianapolis acquisition. Free cash flow conversion has averaged 71% across the period.
INVESTMENT THESIS

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

Second, the end markets HPC serves are structurally attractive. The orthopaedic implants market is forecast to grow at 5–6% annually through 2030, driven by ageing demographics in Europe and the United States. Aerospace component demand is recovering strongly post-COVID, with Airbus and Boeing collectively targeting build-rate increases of approximately 40% over the next five years. Semiconductor capital equipment demand is more cyclical, but HPC's exposure is weighted toward EUV-related components, where structural demand growth is robust.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

Fourth, we see meaningful M&A opportunity. The European precision machining sector remains highly fragmented, with the top 10 players accounting for less than 30% of the market. We have already identified five actionable targets in the EUR 30–80 million enterprise value range that would be accretive on both growth and margin grounds. The founding family has historically been reluctant to pursue M&A; under our ownership we expect to complete two to three add-on acquisitions over the holding period.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. We are comfortable with this exposure given (a) the structural growth in EUV, and (b) HPC's flexible cost base, which allowed the Company to maintain EBITDA margins above 15% throughout the 2023 downturn.

Customer concentration is a watch item. HPC's largest customer, a global orthopaedic implants manufacturer, accounted for 18% of revenue in 2024. While the relationship is multi-decade and contractually backed by long-term supply agreements, any meaningful disruption to this account would materially impact Company performance.

Foreign exchange exposure is significant. Approximately 55% of revenue is denominated in EUR, 30% in USD, and the remainder in CHF and other currencies. Cost base is more heavily CHF-weighted given the Swiss manufacturing footprint. CHF strength against EUR over the past three years has cost HPC roughly 180 basis points of cumulative margin. We expect to hedge transaction exposure systematically post-close and have factored a normalised CHF/EUR rate of 0.98 into our base case.

Founder transition risk is moderate. Andreas Schiller, son of the founder, has served as CEO for 17 years and will step back to the board post-close. The Company has identified an internal successor — Petra Köhler, currently COO — who is well-regarded by the management team and customers. We have completed extensive reference checks. Andreas Schiller has committed to remain on the board for the first three years post-close and will rollover approximately 8% of his proceeds into the transaction.

Revenue growth of 9% CAGR, taking 2024 revenue of EUR 587 million to approximately EUR 905 million by 2029. This growth is composed of: 5% organic growth in line with end-market expansion, 2% from share gain in medical implants, and 2% from contemplated M&A.

EBITDA margin expansion from 17.5% to 21.0% over the hold period, delivering EBITDA of approximately EUR 190 million by 2029. The margin lift is sourced from the footprint consolidation programme (approximately 120 bps), procurement initiatives (approximately 80 bps), automation investment in Brno (approximately 60 bps), and operating leverage on incremental revenue (approximately 60 bps).

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 11.0x EBITDA, marginally below the entry multiple, reflecting prudence regarding sector multiples five years forward. In our upside case, multiple expansion to 12.5x reflects the higher-margin, more diversified, larger-scale platform we expect HPC to become.

The base case generates a 2.4x gross MOIC and a 19% gross IRR. The upside case generates 3.1x gross MOIC and 24% gross IRR. The downside case — in which margin expansion delivers only 150 bps and revenue growth is held at 5% — generates 1.7x gross MOIC and 11% gross IRR.
MANAGEMENT AND ORGANISATION

Petra Köhler, age 49, will become CEO upon close. She joined HPC in 2009 from Sulzer, where she ran the rotating equipment business. She has held the COO role at HPC since 2018 and is credited internally with the success of the Indianapolis integration. Reference checks across customers, suppliers, and former colleagues have been uniformly positive.

The CFO, Markus Zehnder, has been with HPC for 11 years and is well-regarded. We see no need to change this role. We will recruit a Chief Commercial Officer post-close — a role HPC has historically not had — to coordinate the global customer interface across the three end markets. We have already identified a strong candidate currently working in a senior commercial role at GF Machining Solutions.

The broader management team is mature, but we have identified the procurement function as under-resourced relative to the Company's scale and complexity. A Chief Procurement Officer will be recruited in year one, with a mandate to deliver the EUR 8–12 million of annualised procurement savings identified in diligence.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

The Schiller family will retain a 15% economic interest. Management will hold the remaining 7%. We have negotiated standard tag-along and drag-along rights, and a clear governance framework giving Halden Group majority board representation (3 of 5 seats).

Diligence has been thorough. We engaged Bain & Company on commercial diligence (six weeks, completed late February), Deloitte on financial and tax diligence, Kirkland & Ellis on legal, and ERM on ESG and environmental diligence. The Bain report — circulated separately — confirms our market positioning thesis and identifies an additional EUR 14 million of revenue synergies from cross-selling between segments that we have not underwritten in the base case.

We have agreed exclusivity through 31 March 2025 and expect to sign definitive documentation by 28 March. Closing is targeted for mid-June, subject to merger control clearances in the EU, US, and Switzerland. No competition issues are anticipated.

HPC represents an attractive opportunity to acquire a category leader in a structurally growing market with a clear operational improvement plan and proven through-cycle resilience. The base case returns of 2.4x / 19% are in line with our private equity portfolio benchmarks, and we see meaningful upside optionality from M&A and end-market acceleration. The risks are well-understood and manageable. We recommend approval.

Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

The Schiller family will retain a 15% economic interest. Management will hold the remaining 7%. We have negotiated standard tag-along and drag-along rights, and a clear governance framework giving Halden Group majority board representation (3 of 5 seats).
CLOSING CONSIDERATIONS

Diligence has been thorough. We engaged Bain & Company on commercial diligence (six weeks, completed late February), Deloitte on financial and tax diligence, Kirkland & Ellis on legal, and ERM on ESG and environmental diligence. The Bain report — circulated separately — confirms our market positioning thesis and identifies an additional EUR 14 million of revenue synergies from cross-selling between segments that we have not underwritten in the base case.

We have agreed exclusivity through 31 March 2025 and expect to sign definitive documentation by 28 March. Closing is targeted for mid-June, subject to merger control clearances in the EU, US, and Switzerland. No competition issues are anticipated.

HPC represents an attractive opportunity to acquire a category leader in a structurally growing market with a clear operational improvement plan and proven through-cycle resilience. The base case returns of 2.4x / 19% are in line with our private equity portfolio benchmarks, and we see meaningful upside optionality from M&A and end-market acceleration. The risks are well-understood and manageable. We recommend approval.

The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

Second, the end markets HPC serves are structurally attractive. The orthopaedic implants market is forecast to grow at 5–6% annually through 2030, driven by ageing demographics in Europe and the United States. Aerospace component demand is recovering strongly post-COVID, with Airbus and Boeing collectively targeting build-rate increases of approximately 40% over the next five years. Semiconductor capital equipment demand is more cyclical, but HPC's exposure is weighted toward EUV-related components, where structural demand growth is robust.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The founding family has historically been reluctant to pursue M&A; under our ownership we expect to complete two to three add-on acquisitions over the holding period.

occurrences.extract: We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC has grown revenue from EUR 312 million in 2020 to EUR 587 million in 2024, a compound annual growth rate of 17.1%. EBITDA over the same period has expanded from EUR 48 million to EUR 103 million, with margins improving from 15.4% to 17.5%. Growth has been split roughly evenly between organic share gains and the contribution from the Indianapolis acquisition. Free cash flow conversion has averaged 71% across the period.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. To:        Global Investment Committee
From:      European Industrials Team — Stefan Brunner (Partner), Lena Hofmann (Member of Management), Tobias Reichmann (Senior Vice President)
Date:      14 March 2025
Subject:   Project Alpine — Proposed acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG
RECOMMENDATION

We seek approval for Halden Group to invest up to EUR 480 million of equity in the acquisition of Helvetia Precision Components AG ("HPC" or "the Company"), a Zurich-headquartered manufacturer of high-precision machined components for the medical devices, aerospace, and semiconductor end markets. The transaction values HPC at an enterprise value of EUR 1.15 billion, representing 11.2x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 103 million. Halden Group would acquire a 78% controlling stake from the founding Schiller family, with the remainder retained by management. The seller is being advised by Lincoln International.

HPC was founded in 1962 by Werner Schiller in Winterthur. The Company manufactures complex precision components — typically machined to tolerances of 5 microns or tighter — for applications where failure is not an option. Roughly 48% of revenue is generated from medical device customers, primarily orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments. A further 32% comes from aerospace, split between civil aviation engine components and defence applications. The remaining 20% serves semiconductor capital equipment manufacturers, where HPC supplies critical components used in wafer fabrication tools.

The Company operates four manufacturing facilities: a headquarters site in Winterthur (Switzerland), a larger production facility in Olten (Switzerland), a US operation in Indianapolis acquired in 2018, and a smaller Czech facility in Brno established in 2021 to serve European aerospace customers at lower cost. Total headcount stands at 1,420 employees, of whom approximately 240 are based outside Switzerland.

HPC has grown revenue from EUR 312 million in 2020 to EUR 587 million in 2024, a compound annual growth rate of 17.1%. EBITDA over the same period has expanded from EUR 48 million to EUR 103 million, with margins improving from 15.4% to 17.5%. Growth has been split roughly evenly between organic share gains and the contribution from the Indianapolis acquisition. Free cash flow conversion has averaged 71% across the period.
INVESTMENT THESIS

First, the Company occupies an enviable competitive position. In its core medical implants vertical, HPC is one of three qualified suppliers globally for hip and knee replacement components meeting both FDA Class II and EU MDR requirements at scale. Switching costs for medical device OEMs are substantial — qualification of a new supplier typically takes 18 to 24 months and involves clinical trial impact assessments. As a result, customer relationships are durable: HPC's top 10 customers have been with the Company for an average of 14 years, and revenue retention from these accounts has been 102% over the past five years.

Second, the end markets HPC serves are structurally attractive. The orthopaedic implants market is forecast to grow at 5–6% annually through 2030, driven by ageing demographics in Europe and the United States. Aerospace component demand is recovering strongly post-COVID, with Airbus and Boeing collectively targeting build-rate increases of approximately 40% over the next five years. Semiconductor capital equipment demand is more cyclical, but HPC's exposure is weighted toward EUV-related components, where structural demand growth is robust.

Third, there is a clear margin expansion path. HPC's current EBITDA margin of 17.5% trails best-in-class peers (Burckhardt Compression at 19.8%, VAT Group at 31.2% — though VAT operates in a different segment) and our diligence has identified a coherent set of operational levers we believe can deliver 300 to 400 basis points of margin uplift over five years. The principal levers are: footprint consolidation in Switzerland (closing the Winterthur facility and absorbing volumes into Olten), procurement consolidation across the now-fragmented supplier base inherited from the Indianapolis acquisition, and a programme of automation investment in the Brno facility.

Fourth, we see meaningful M&A opportunity. The European precision machining sector remains highly fragmented, with the top 10 players accounting for less than 30% of the market. We have already identified five actionable targets in the EUR 30–80 million enterprise value range that would be accretive on both growth and margin grounds. The founding family has historically been reluctant to pursue M&A; under our ownership we expect to complete two to three add-on acquisitions over the holding period.

The semiconductor exposure introduces cyclicality that the medical and aerospace segments do not. In the 2023 downcycle, HPC's semiconductor revenue declined by 28% year-on-year, though overall Company revenue still grew due to offsetting strength in the other segments. We are comfortable with this exposure given (a) the structural growth in EUV, and (b) HPC's flexible cost base, which allowed the Company to maintain EBITDA margins above 15% throughout the 2023 downturn.

Customer concentration is a watch item. HPC's largest customer, a global orthopaedic implants manufacturer, accounted for 18% of revenue in 2024. While the relationship is multi-decade and contractually backed by long-term supply agreements, any meaningful disruption to this account would materially impact Company performance.

Foreign exchange exposure is significant. Approximately 55% of revenue is denominated in EUR, 30% in USD, and the remainder in CHF and other currencies. Cost base is more heavily CHF-weighted given the Swiss manufacturing footprint. CHF strength against EUR over the past three years has cost HPC roughly 180 basis points of cumulative margin. We expect to hedge transaction exposure systematically post-close and have factored a normalised CHF/EUR rate of 0.98 into our base case.

Founder transition risk is moderate. Andreas Schiller, son of the founder, has served as CEO for 17 years and will step back to the board post-close. The Company has identified an internal successor — Petra Köhler, currently COO — who is well-regarded by the management team and customers. We have completed extensive reference checks. Andreas Schiller has committed to remain on the board for the first three years post-close and will rollover approximately 8% of his proceeds into the transaction.

Revenue growth of 9% CAGR, taking 2024 revenue of EUR 587 million to approximately EUR 905 million by 2029. This growth is composed of: 5% organic growth in line with end-market expansion, 2% from share gain in medical implants, and 2% from contemplated M&A.

EBITDA margin expansion from 17.5% to 21.0% over the hold period, delivering EBITDA of approximately EUR 190 million by 2029. The margin lift is sourced from the footprint consolidation programme (approximately 120 bps), procurement initiatives (approximately 80 bps), automation investment in Brno (approximately 60 bps), and operating leverage on incremental revenue (approximately 60 bps).

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 11.0x EBITDA, marginally below the entry multiple, reflecting prudence regarding sector multiples five years forward. In our upside case, multiple expansion to 12.5x reflects the higher-margin, more diversified, larger-scale platform we expect HPC to become.

The base case generates a 2.4x gross MOIC and a 19% gross IRR. The upside case generates 3.1x gross MOIC and 24% gross IRR. The downside case — in which margin expansion delivers only 150 bps and revenue growth is held at 5% — generates 1.7x gross MOIC and 11% gross IRR.
MANAGEMENT AND ORGANISATION

Petra Köhler, age 49, will become CEO upon close. She joined HPC in 2009 from Sulzer, where she ran the rotating equipment business. She has held the COO role at HPC since 2018 and is credited internally with the success of the Indianapolis integration. Reference checks across customers, suppliers, and former colleagues have been uniformly positive.

The CFO, Markus Zehnder, has been with HPC for 11 years and is well-regarded. We see no need to change this role. We will recruit a Chief Commercial Officer post-close — a role HPC has historically not had — to coordinate the global customer interface across the three end markets. We have already identified a strong candidate currently working in a senior commercial role at GF Machining Solutions.

The broader management team is mature, but we have identified the procurement function as under-resourced relative to the Company's scale and complexity. A Chief Procurement Officer will be recruited in year one, with a mandate to deliver the EUR 8–12 million of annualised procurement savings identified in diligence.

The transaction will be funded with EUR 480 million of equity from Halden Group, EUR 130 million of equity from co-investors (currently anticipated to include two existing LP relationships), and EUR 540 million of senior and second-lien debt. Total leverage at close is approximately 5.2x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriate given the Company's cash generation profile and recession-resilient end-market mix. Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse have provided fully underwritten commitments.

The Schiller family will retain a 15% economic interest. Management will hold the remaining 7%. We have negotiated standard tag-along and drag-along rights, and a clear governance framework giving Halden Group majority board representation (3 of 5 seats).

Diligence has been thorough. We engaged Bain & Company on commercial diligence (six weeks, completed late February), Deloitte on financial and tax diligence, Kirkland & Ellis on legal, and ERM on ESG and environmental diligence. The Bain report — circulated separately — confirms our market positioning thesis and identifies an additional EUR 14 million of revenue synergies from cross-selling between segments that we have not underwritten in the base case.

We have agreed exclusivity through 31 March 2025 and expect to sign definitive documentation by 28 March. Closing is targeted for mid-June, subject to merger control clearances in the EU, US, and Switzerland. No competition issues are anticipated.

HPC represents an attractive opportunity to acquire a category leader in a structurally growing market with a clear operational improvement plan and proven through-cycle resilience. The base case returns of 2.4x / 19% are in line with our private equity portfolio benchmarks, and we see meaningful upside optionality from M&A and end-market acceleration. The risks are well-understood and manageable. We recommend approval.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The deal thesis comes through clearly and the structure works well. The competitive position is grounded in something concrete and verifiable - the point that the Company is one of three qualified suppliers for FDA Class II and MDR hip and knee components, with 18 to 24 month qualification cycles, does the heavy lifting that an LP memo of this kind needs. The growth and margin history is presented cleanly, and the four-pillar value creation plan is specific enough to be useful rather than generic, particularly the M&A section where you name a bounded target universe and an EV range.

The weaker stretch is the risk paragraph. Writing that semiconductor cyclicality, customer concentration, FX, and the founder transition are 'each is understood and reflected in our planning, with specific mitigations in place' tells the reader nothing and will stand out precisely because the rest of the memo is specific. I would give each risk a sentence, even a short one, especially the founder transition given the Schiller family is retaining 22%. I would also tighten the bridge between the pillars and the returns - the pillars imply margin uplift of 300-400 bps plus 9% revenue growth plus M&A, and it is not obvious how that reconciles to 2.4x and 19%, so a reader doing the arithmetic may come away unsure whether the base case is conservative or stretched. One more thing worth a look: the 'International margin expansion' label on the first pillar reads oddly when the substance is Swiss footprint consolidation and procurement, which are not really international levers.

reading.writerFeedback:
The update reads clearly and lands the key point early - we are modestly ahead on both revenue and EBITDA, the leadership transition is holding, and the base case is unchanged. The structure of good news first, then the two watch items, then the operational milestones works well, and the specificity on Köhler's priorities and Wenger's early procurement wins gives the reader confidence that execution is real rather than rhetorical.

The weaker stretch is the semiconductor paragraph, which asserts rather than explains. Saying "Our base case returns remain intact but the segment will be a moderating factor through 2026" after a EUR 17 million revenue cut needs a sentence on why the overall case still holds - is medical offsetting it, is the margin mix helping, or is 2027 recovery assumed? Similarly, the quality issue at the second-largest medical customer deserves one more line on root cause and whether enhanced monitoring puts any share of wallet at risk, because "The financial impact is small" addresses only the direct cost. Lehmann's arrival as CCO is noted but given no content at all - either say what she is tasked with or drop her to the next update.

sentences.text: Six months after closing, our investment in Helvetia Precision Components is tracking modestly ahead of underwriting.

occurrences.extract: Six-Month Post-Close Review

Six months into our investment in HPC, performance is tracking modestly ahead of the base case underwritten at IC. Revenue for the period reached EUR 318 million, 4% above plan. EBITDA of EUR 58 million was 7% above plan, with margins of 18.3% reflecting early traction on the procurement programme and favourable mix. The leadership transition has proceeded smoothly, with Petra Köhler establishing herself well as CEO. Two material risks have emerged that we are actively managing: a slowdown in semiconductor capital equipment orders, and an unexpected quality issue at one medical device customer.

M&A pipeline: We have advanced two of the five targets identified pre-close. The first — a French specialist in titanium machining — is in second-round bids; we expect to know within six weeks whether we have been selected. The second — a German family business in optical components — has agreed to enter exclusivity in January 2026 at a preliminary valuation of EUR 42 million.

Six months into our investment in HPC, performance is tracking modestly ahead of the base case underwritten at IC. Revenue for the period reached EUR 318 million, 4% above plan. The leadership transition has proceeded smoothly, with Petra Köhler establishing herself well as CEO. Two material risks have emerged that we are actively managing: a slowdown in semiconductor capital equipment orders, and an unexpected quality issue at one medical device customer.

occurrences.extract: Period: June 2025 – November 2025

The CEO transition has gone better than expected. Petra Köhler took over from Andreas Schiller on 16 June and has moved decisively on early priorities — restructuring the procurement function, initiating the Winterthur footprint review, and establishing a monthly operating cadence with the Halden Group team. Andreas Schiller has integrated comfortably into his board role and continues to provide useful customer-facing support.

Winterthur footprint review: Site closure is now under formal consultation with the workforce, with a target closure date of June 2026. Approximately 180 roles are affected; roughly 60 are expected to transfer to Olten. The associated restructuring charge of EUR 22 million has been provided in the period. We expect annualised savings of EUR 14 million from full transition, slightly above our underwriting estimate of EUR 12 million.

The next major milestones are: completion of the French add-on (Q1 2026), Brno automation phase one going live (Q3 2026), and Winterthur consolidation completion (mid-2026). We will provide a further detailed update at the 12-month review in June 2026.

occurrences.extract: PORTFOLIO COMPANY UPDATE — STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL

Six months into our investment in HPC, performance is tracking modestly ahead of the base case underwritten at IC. Revenue for the period reached EUR 318 million, 4% above plan. EBITDA of EUR 58 million was 7% above plan, with margins of 18.3% reflecting early traction on the procurement programme and favourable mix. The leadership transition has proceeded smoothly, with Petra Köhler establishing herself well as CEO. Two material risks have emerged that we are actively managing: a slowdown in semiconductor capital equipment orders, and an unexpected quality issue at one medical device customer.

We have recruited two of the three new senior hires planned in our underwriting. Klaus Wenger joined as Chief Procurement Officer in September, having previously held the same role at Belimo. He brings strong category management discipline that the Company has historically lacked. Sophie Lehmann joined as Chief Commercial Officer in October from GF Machining Solutions. The remaining priority hire — a VP of Digital and Automation — is in late-stage interviews with two strong candidates; we expect this role to be filled by end-Q1 2026.

Period revenue of EUR 318 million represents growth of 11% versus the prior comparable period. The medical implants segment grew 14%, well ahead of expectations, driven by a 22% increase from our largest orthopaedic customer following their successful US product launch. Aerospace revenue grew 9%, broadly in line with build-rate increases at Airbus. Semiconductor revenue declined 6% in the period, reflecting weaker orders from two key customers (see Risks section below).

EBITDA of EUR 58 million versus a budget of EUR 54 million was driven by three factors: favourable mix (the strength in medical was higher-margin than budgeted), early procurement wins (Klaus Wenger has already secured EUR 2.1 million of annualised savings against a year-one target of EUR 5 million), and modest favourable FX (CHF weakened to 1.02 against EUR over the period, against our base case of 0.98).

Cash conversion was 68%, slightly below the 71% historical average, reflecting a planned working capital build to support the medical segment ramp. Net debt at period end stood at EUR 512 million, down EUR 28 million from close.

Procurement programme: Klaus Wenger has built a 90-day diagnostic. He has identified EUR 11 million of addressable savings across consolidation, demand management, and renegotiation — broadly in line with our diligence estimate. EUR 2.1 million is now contracted; he expects to be at a EUR 6 million annualised run-rate by mid-2026.

M&A pipeline: We have advanced two of the five targets identified pre-close. The first — a French specialist in titanium machining — is in second-round bids; we expect to know within six weeks whether we have been selected. The second — a German family business in optical components — has agreed to enter exclusivity in January 2026 at a preliminary valuation of EUR 42 million.

Semiconductor slowdown: We flagged this as a cyclical risk in our underwriting and the early signals are now visible. Two semiconductor capital equipment customers have pushed orders by one to two quarters. We do not expect a deep downturn — the demand picture for EUV remains structurally strong — but we are guiding to flat semiconductor revenue for the next 12 months and have adjusted our full-year forecast accordingly. The full-year 2026 budget assumes semiconductor revenue of EUR 105 million versus our original underwriting of EUR 122 million.

Medical device customer quality issue: In October, our second-largest medical customer raised a quality concern relating to a specific component lot manufactured in the Olten facility. Initial root cause analysis points to a tooling wear issue that was not detected by in-process inspection. The cost impact to HPC is limited — approximately EUR 3 million in returns, rework, and credit — but the relationship cost is more significant. Petra Köhler met the customer's COO in November and the customer is satisfied with the corrective action plan. However the customer has placed HPC on enhanced quality monitoring for 12 months, which is an unwelcome development. We are tracking this closely.

We remain confident in our base case returns of 2.4x MOIC and 19% IRR. The early traction on procurement and the strength in medical implants are partial offsets to the semiconductor weakness and the customer quality issue. We do not at this stage see reason to revise our underwriting.

Semiconductor slowdown: We flagged this as a cyclical risk in our underwriting and the early signals are now visible. Two semiconductor capital equipment customers have pushed orders by one to two quarters. We do not expect a deep downturn — the demand picture for EUV remains structurally strong — but we are guiding to flat semiconductor revenue for the next 12 months and have adjusted our full-year forecast accordingly. The full-year 2026 budget assumes semiconductor revenue of EUR 105 million versus our original underwriting of EUR 122 million.

Medical device customer quality issue: In October, our second-largest medical customer raised a quality concern relating to a specific component lot manufactured in the Olten facility. Initial root cause analysis points to a tooling wear issue that was not detected by in-process inspection. The cost impact to HPC is limited — approximately EUR 3 million in returns, rework, and credit — but the relationship cost is more significant. Petra Köhler met the customer's COO in November and the customer is satisfied with the corrective action plan. However the customer has placed HPC on enhanced quality monitoring for 12 months, which is an unwelcome development. We are tracking this closely.

CHF strength: Although the CHF has weakened modestly through the period, the structural Swiss currency exposure remains a concern. We have implemented a 12-month rolling hedge programme covering 70% of EUR revenue exposure. We expect to extend this to 24 months over the course of 2026.

The next major milestones are: completion of the French add-on (Q1 2026), Brno automation phase one going live (Q3 2026), and Winterthur consolidation completion (mid-2026). We will provide a further detailed update at the 12-month review in June 2026.
