sentences.text: Klaus Wenger joined as Chief Procurement Officer in September and has already secured EUR 2.1 million of annualised savings, against a year-one target of EUR 5 million.

occurrences.extract: We have recruited two of the three new senior hires planned in our underwriting. Klaus Wenger joined as Chief Procurement Officer in September, having previously held the same role at Belimo. He brings strong category management discipline that the Company has historically lacked. Sophie Lehmann joined as Chief Commercial Officer in October from GF Machining Solutions. The remaining priority hire — a VP of Digital and Automation — is in late-stage interviews with two strong candidates; we expect this role to be filled by end-Q1 2026.

EBITDA of EUR 58 million versus a budget of EUR 54 million was driven by three factors: favourable mix (the strength in medical was higher-margin than budgeted), early procurement wins (Klaus Wenger has already secured EUR 2.1 million of annualised savings against a year-one target of EUR 5 million), and modest favourable FX (CHF weakened to 1.02 against EUR over the period, against our base case of 0.98).

Procurement programme: Klaus Wenger has built a 90-day diagnostic. He has identified EUR 11 million of addressable savings across consolidation, demand management, and renegotiation — broadly in line with our diligence estimate. EUR 2.1 million is now contracted; he expects to be at a EUR 6 million annualised run-rate by mid-2026.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The update reads clearly and lands the key point early - we are modestly ahead on both revenue and EBITDA, the leadership transition is holding, and the base case is unchanged. The structure of good news first, then the two watch items, then the operational milestones works well, and the specificity on Köhler's priorities and Wenger's early procurement wins gives the reader confidence that execution is real rather than rhetorical.

The weaker stretch is the semiconductor paragraph, which asserts rather than explains. Saying "Our base case returns remain intact but the segment will be a moderating factor through 2026" after a EUR 17 million revenue cut needs a sentence on why the overall case still holds - is medical offsetting it, is the margin mix helping, or is 2027 recovery assumed? Similarly, the quality issue at the second-largest medical customer deserves one more line on root cause and whether enhanced monitoring puts any share of wallet at risk, because "The financial impact is small" addresses only the direct cost. Lehmann's arrival as CCO is noted but given no content at all - either say what she is tasked with or drop her to the next update.

reading.writerFeedback:
The release reads cleanly and hits the key marks a reader expects: what was bought, where it operates, who runs it, and how it fits the platform. The positioning of Lumen as a high-purity player serving semiconductor and pharma end-markets comes through clearly, and anchoring the deal as the eighth investment from the European Industrials strategy alongside the EUR 2 billion sector tally gives useful context on Meridian's conviction in the space.

The weaker element is that the value-creation plan is thin and generic. 'Meridian intends to support an acceleration of the Company's expansion strategy, with a focus on the Asian electronics market and on selective acquisitions in adjacent specialty chemical categories' could be said about almost any sponsor-backed chemicals platform - it would benefit from a concrete hook, whether that is a target geography, a capacity expansion, or the type of bolt-on in mind. I would also push for at least one quote, ideally from Dr. Brandt or the Meridian deal lead, since the current draft has no human voice at all. Finally, the omission of deal size, seller, and closing date is conspicuous; if any of those can be disclosed, the release will land harder.

occurrences.extract: Meridian Capital completes acquisition of Lumen Specialty Chemicals

Frankfurt, Germany — 8 October 2025 — Meridian Capital ("Meridian"), the global private markets firm, today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of Lumen Specialty Chemicals GmbH ("Lumen" or "the Company"), a leading European producer of high-purity specialty chemicals for the electronics, pharmaceutical, and advanced materials industries. The transaction was first announced in June 2025.

"Lumen represents exactly the type of investment opportunity Meridian is built to pursue," said Henrik Vossberg, Partner and Head of European Industrials at Meridian Capital. "It is a category-leading business serving structurally growing end markets, with a strong management team and meaningful opportunities for operational improvement and international expansion. We are delighted to partner with the Lumen team on the next phase of growth."

The acquisition is the eighth investment from Meridian's flagship European Industrials strategy and brings the firm's total invested capital in the specialty chemicals sector to over EUR 2 billion across its global platforms.
About Meridian Capital

Meridian Capital is a global private markets firm with EUR 95 billion in assets under management. The firm invests in private equity, infrastructure, and private credit across Europe, North America, and Asia, on behalf of institutional and private wealth clients. Founded in 2002 and headquartered in Zurich, Meridian employs over 1,400 professionals across 14 offices worldwide.
Meridian Capital — Sarah Bauer, sarah.bauer@meridiancapital.example, +41 41 555 0100

occurrences.extract: Frankfurt, Germany — 8 October 2025 — Meridian Capital ("Meridian"), the global private markets firm, today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of Lumen Specialty Chemicals GmbH ("Lumen" or "the Company"), a leading European producer of high-purity specialty chemicals for the electronics, pharmaceutical, and advanced materials industries. The transaction was first announced in June 2025.

Headquartered in Frankfurt, Lumen operates three production facilities across Germany and Belgium and employs approximately 850 people. occurrences.extract: Meridian Capital completes acquisition of Lumen Specialty Chemicals

Frankfurt, Germany — 8 October 2025 — Meridian Capital ("Meridian"), the global private markets firm, today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of Lumen Specialty Chemicals GmbH ("Lumen" or "the Company"), a leading European producer of high-purity specialty chemicals for the electronics, pharmaceutical, and advanced materials industries. The transaction was first announced in June 2025.

"Lumen represents exactly the type of investment opportunity Meridian is built to pursue," said Henrik Vossberg, Partner and Head of European Industrials at Meridian Capital. "It is a category-leading business serving structurally growing end markets, with a strong management team and meaningful opportunities for operational improvement and international expansion. We are delighted to partner with the Lumen team on the next phase of growth."

Lumen will be led by its existing Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Annika Brandt, who has held the role since 2019. The senior management team will remain in place. Meridian will support the Company's expansion strategy, with particular focus on the rapidly growing Asian electronics market and on selective acquisitions in adjacent specialty chemical categories.

"This is an important milestone for Lumen," said Dr. Annika Brandt, Chief Executive Officer of Lumen Specialty Chemicals. "Meridian brings deep expertise in our industry and a long-term perspective that aligns with our growth ambitions. Together we will accelerate our investment in capacity expansion, technology, and the talented people who make Lumen what it is."

The acquisition is the eighth investment from Meridian's flagship European Industrials strategy and brings the firm's total invested capital in the specialty chemicals sector to over EUR 2 billion across its global platforms.
Meridian was advised by Rothschild & Co (financial), Hengeler Mueller (legal), and Roland Berger (commercial). The seller was advised by Lazard.

The firm invests in private equity, infrastructure, and private credit across Europe, North America, and Asia, on behalf of institutional and private wealth clients. Founded in 2002 and headquartered in Zurich, Meridian employs over 1,400 professionals across 14 offices worldwide.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The release reads cleanly and hits the key marks a reader expects: what was bought, where it operates, who runs it, and how it fits the platform. The positioning of Lumen as a high-purity player serving semiconductor and pharma end-markets comes through clearly, and anchoring the deal as the eighth investment from the European Industrials strategy alongside the EUR 2 billion sector tally gives useful context on Meridian's conviction in the space.

The weaker element is that the value-creation plan is thin and generic. 'Meridian intends to support an acceleration of the Company's expansion strategy, with a focus on the Asian electronics market and on selective acquisitions in adjacent specialty chemical categories' could be said about almost any sponsor-backed chemicals platform - it would benefit from a concrete hook, whether that is a target geography, a capacity expansion, or the type of bolt-on in mind. I would also push for at least one quote, ideally from Dr. Brandt or the Meridian deal lead, since the current draft has no human voice at all. Finally, the omission of deal size, seller, and closing date is conspicuous; if any of those can be disclosed, the release will land harder.

reading.writerFeedback:
The draft tells the NorTech story well. The arc from entry to exit is clear, the value creation levers are laid out in a logical sequence, and the headline numbers land with impact. The competitive tension in the process - "Brookfield's SEK 18.4 billion bid meaningfully ahead of the next bid at SEK 16.9 billion" - is a nice detail that reinforces the quality of the outcome, and tying the single realization to the move in Fund IV's net IRR from 16.8% to 19.7% is exactly the frame LPs will want.

That said, a few things need work. The claim that "Fund IV becomes one of our strongest vintages" is asserted rather than supported - give it a comparative anchor or drop it. The operational section reads as a list rather than a narrative; the line "Manufacturing footprint optimisation and the new Polish facility completed the operational picture" is filler and should either be fleshed out or cut. The closing pivot to Fund V deployment is abrupt and deserves a sentence of substance rather than a sign-off. Finally, the management-support point is useful but the phrasing "an additional factor in the Company's preference" is soft - say plainly whether this influenced price, certainty, or both.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The draft tells the NorTech story well. The arc from entry to exit is clear, the value creation levers are laid out in a logical sequence, and the headline numbers land with impact. The competitive tension in the process - "Brookfield's SEK 18.4 billion bid meaningfully ahead of the next bid at SEK 16.9 billion" - is a nice detail that reinforces the quality of the outcome, and tying the single realization to the move in Fund IV's net IRR from 16.8% to 19.7% is exactly the frame LPs will want.

That said, a few things need work. The claim that "Fund IV becomes one of our strongest vintages" is asserted rather than supported - give it a comparative anchor or drop it. The operational section reads as a list rather than a narrative; the line "Manufacturing footprint optimisation and the new Polish facility completed the operational picture" is filler and should either be fleshed out or cut. The closing pivot to Fund V deployment is abrupt and deserves a sentence of substance rather than a sign-off. Finally, the management-support point is useful but the phrasing "an additional factor in the Company's preference" is soft - say plainly whether this influenced price, certainty, or both.

reading.writerFeedback:
The arc works well and the human beat lands - naming Magnus and Mikael with a specific contribution for each gives the piece warmth without tipping into sentimentality, and the pivot line "The numbers tell one story; the team's transformation tells the bigger one" earns its place. The geographic and financial progression is clear enough that a reader skimming will still take away the core story.

The weak spot is the opening, which buries the deal and reads flatly: "Meridian Capital has completed the sale of NorTech Industries to Brookfield this week" - we should lead with something that signals why this exit matters, not just that it happened. I would also tighten the metrics presentation, since "grown from a fifth of total revenue at entry to more than 40 percent at exit" mixes a fraction and a figure in a way that makes the jump harder to feel than it should be. One more pass to sharpen the top and align the comparisons would lift it.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The arc works well and the human beat lands - naming Magnus and Mikael with a specific contribution for each gives the piece warmth without tipping into sentimentality, and the pivot line "The numbers tell one story; the team's transformation tells the bigger one" earns its place. The geographic and financial progression is clear enough that a reader skimming will still take away the core story.

The weak spot is the opening, which buries the deal and reads flatly: "Meridian Capital has completed the sale of NorTech Industries to Brookfield this week" - we should lead with something that signals why this exit matters, not just that it happened. I would also tighten the metrics presentation, since "grown from a fifth of total revenue at entry to more than 40 percent at exit" mixes a fraction and a figure in a way that makes the jump harder to feel than it should be. One more pass to sharpen the top and align the comparisons would lift it.

reading.writerFeedback:
The core investment case comes through clearly and the structural arguments hang together well. The three-point framing on market penetration, switching costs, and headroom from 8.6% to a 14'000-forwarder TAM is the strongest passage, and the ARR trajectory from EUR 52 million to EUR 84 million gives the growth story real credibility. The team and footprint detail is also useful context.

That said, the draft is thin where it should be sharpest. The returns section - "Our base case generates 2.6x MOIC and 21% gross IRR" - is asserted without any bridge from the 19% ARR CAGR to the exit, and there is no mention of exit multiple assumption, leverage, or margin expansion path. The 11.1% EBITDA margin sits awkwardly next to a EUR 445 million entry without a word on the path to profitability at scale. There is also an internal inconsistency worth resolving: ARR is given as EUR 84 million as of October 2025 in one line and EUR 81 million "today" in the projection line. Finally, the risks section is simply missing - competition from legacy incumbents is named as a strength but never tested as a threat, and there is nothing on customer concentration, FX, or integration risk from the Bangalore build-out. I would push for a dedicated risks and mitigants paragraph before this goes to IC.

sentences.text: CloudPivot Systems (the "Company") is a London-headquartered vertical SaaS platform for the European freight forwarding industry.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Borealis — Proposed acquisition of CloudPivot Systems Limited

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 285 million for a 64% controlling stake in CloudPivot Systems Limited ("CloudPivot" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered vertical SaaS platform serving the European logistics and freight forwarding industry. The transaction values CloudPivot at an enterprise value of EUR 445 million. On a trailing basis the Company generates an EBITDA margin of approximately 13%, reflecting continued investment in product and go-to-market.

Vertical SaaS economics. Freight forwarding is a deeply specialised industry with workflow patterns that horizontal ERP systems handle poorly. CloudPivot's product reflects ten years of domain investment and is genuinely differentiated. The closest international comparable, US-focused CargoOne, was acquired by Thoma Bravo in early 2024 at 11x ARR.

Mission-critical software with very low churn. Once a forwarder is operating on CloudPivot, switching costs are very high. The platform integrates with customs authorities, carrier networks, and customer systems; reverting to alternative software would mean rebuilding all of these integrations. Gross retention of 94% reflects this.

occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 285 million for a 64% controlling stake in CloudPivot Systems Limited ("CloudPivot" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered vertical SaaS platform serving the European logistics and freight forwarding industry. The transaction values CloudPivot at an enterprise value of EUR 445 million. On a trailing basis the Company generates an EBITDA margin of approximately 13%, reflecting continued investment in product and go-to-market.

CloudPivot was founded in London in 2014 by Tom Fairfield (currently CEO) and James O'Brien (currently CTO). The Company provides a comprehensive SaaS platform for freight forwarders and customs brokers, replacing the legacy ERP-style software that dominates the industry. The platform handles shipment booking, customs documentation, rate management, invoicing, and customer portal functionality through a single integrated product.

The Company serves over 1,200 freight forwarder and customs broker customers across 28 European countries. Customers range from single-office operators with 5 to 10 users up to mid-sized regional networks with 200+ users. CloudPivot has not yet meaningfully penetrated the largest global forwarders (Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, DB Schenker, DSV), although a recent pilot with DSV's Italian subsidiary has produced encouraging results.
The Company has been free cash flow positive since 2023. Cash on balance sheet at September 2025 stood at EUR 18 million with no debt.

ARR growth from EUR 81 million today to approximately EUR 195 million over a five-year hold. This represents 19% CAGR, reflecting a measured deceleration from the recent 27% pace as the Company scales.

sentences.text: The team is led by founder-CEO Mr. Tom Fairfield and CTO Mr. James O'Brien.

occurrences.extract: CloudPivot was founded in London in 2014 by Tom Fairfield (currently CEO) and James O'Brien (currently CTO). The Company provides a comprehensive SaaS platform for freight forwarders and customs brokers, replacing the legacy ERP-style software that dominates the industry. The platform handles shipment booking, customs documentation, rate management, invoicing, and customer portal functionality through a single integrated product.

Founder-led with deep industry credibility. Tom Fairfield came from the industry — he ran technology at a mid-sized UK forwarder before founding CloudPivot — and has built a deeply respected position in the European logistics technology community.

Founder transition. CEO Tom Fairfield is 51 and has indicated willingness to remain for the duration of our hold. Should he wish to step back, we have identified the Chief Revenue Officer, Maria Santangelo, as a credible internal successor.

The senior team is strong. Tom Fairfield, CEO, and James O'Brien, CTO, are the co-founders and remain deeply engaged. Maria Santangelo, CRO, joined from HubSpot in 2022 and has rebuilt the European sales organisation. The CFO, Patrick Lawrence, joined from a private equity-backed UK SaaS business in 2024 and has tightened reporting and unit economics discipline.

We will invest EUR 285 million for 64% of the equity. The founders and management will retain 28% in aggregate (Tom Fairfield 14%, James O'Brien 7%, other management 7%) and existing growth equity investor Index Ventures will retain 8%. There is no third-party debt at close. We have negotiated standard governance with majority Halden Group board control (3 of 5 seats).

occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 285 million for a 64% controlling stake in CloudPivot Systems Limited ("CloudPivot" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered vertical SaaS platform serving the European logistics and freight forwarding industry. The transaction values CloudPivot at an enterprise value of EUR 445 million. On a trailing basis the Company generates an EBITDA margin of approximately 13%, reflecting continued investment in product and go-to-market.

The Company serves over 1,200 freight forwarder and customs broker customers across 28 European countries. Customers range from single-office operators with 5 to 10 users up to mid-sized regional networks with 200+ users. CloudPivot has not yet meaningfully penetrated the largest global forwarders (Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, DB Schenker, DSV), although a recent pilot with DSV's Italian subsidiary has produced encouraging results.

Large addressable market with limited modern competition. There are approximately 14,000 freight forwarders and customs brokers in Europe. CloudPivot serves 1,200 of these — an 8.6% penetration rate. The principal competition is fragmented legacy software (Riege, CargoWise — which is the dominant player in larger forwarders — and a long tail of regional incumbents). Most legacy products are visibly aged and customer satisfaction is consistently low.

Founder-led with deep industry credibility. Tom Fairfield came from the industry — he ran technology at a mid-sized UK forwarder before founding CloudPivot — and has built a deeply respected position in the European logistics technology community.

The senior team is strong. Tom Fairfield, CEO, and James O'Brien, CTO, are the co-founders and remain deeply engaged. Maria Santangelo, CRO, joined from HubSpot in 2022 and has rebuilt the European sales organisation. The CFO, Patrick Lawrence, joined from a private equity-backed UK SaaS business in 2024 and has tightened reporting and unit economics discipline.

The total team of 285 people is split approximately as follows: engineering 110, customer success and implementation 75, sales 55, customer support 35, and general & administrative 10. We see opportunities to invest further in product and in mid-market sales capacity in continental Europe.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The core investment case comes through clearly and the structural arguments hang together well. The three-point framing on market penetration, switching costs, and headroom from 8.6% to a 14'000-forwarder TAM is the strongest passage, and the ARR trajectory from EUR 52 million to EUR 84 million gives the growth story real credibility. The team and footprint detail is also useful context.

That said, the draft is thin where it should be sharpest. The returns section - "Our base case generates 2.6x MOIC and 21% gross IRR" - is asserted without any bridge from the 19% ARR CAGR to the exit, and there is no mention of exit multiple assumption, leverage, or margin expansion path. The 11.1% EBITDA margin sits awkwardly next to a EUR 445 million entry without a word on the path to profitability at scale. There is also an internal inconsistency worth resolving: ARR is given as EUR 84 million as of October 2025 in one line and EUR 81 million "today" in the projection line. Finally, the risks section is simply missing - competition from legacy incumbents is named as a strength but never tested as a threat, and there is nothing on customer concentration, FX, or integration risk from the Bangalore build-out. I would push for a dedicated risks and mitigants paragraph before this goes to IC.

reading.writerFeedback:
The thesis is clear and the three-forces structure lands well. The strongest passage is the European distinctiveness argument, where the link from fragmented national leadership to a buy-and-build angle that fits our M&A capability is specific and persuasive. The MDR point is also usefully framed as a barrier that benefits incumbents with existing clearances rather than as generic regulatory colour.

The generative AI section is the weakest part and reads as having it both ways: "The opportunity is for products that genuinely improve clinical workflows" sits next to the claim that AI exposes incumbents to challenger risk, without telling the reader which side we think we are investing on. The reimbursement claim that "payer willingness to reimburse digital health products has improved markedly across the major European markets" is doing a lot of work with no evidence attached, and a sentence or two naming specific schemes would make it much harder to push back on. Finally, the close is softer than it needs to be - if a live opportunity is coming, say so plainly and give the committee a sense of timing.

sentences.text: We are seeing increasing opportunity in European clinical decision support (CDS) software.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Investment thesis — European clinical decision support software

This memo sets out a thematic investment thesis on European clinical decision support ("CDS") software. It is not a transaction memo. We are not yet in dialogue with any specific company. The purpose is to seek Committee endorsement of the thesis itself, which would authorise the team to begin active sourcing and to engage with potential targets at the appropriate level.

The European CDS market is structurally distinct from the US market in several ways. European healthcare is dominated by national payers, which gives CDS products a clearer route to scale once adopted by a national authority. Reimbursement codes for digital health products have improved meaningfully across the major European markets over the past three years. Medical Device Regulation has created higher barriers to entry for serious clinical software, advantaging incumbents who have invested in the regulatory pathway.

We believe the European market is at an inflection point. Three forces are aligning. First, the regulatory pathway under EU MDR is now well-understood and incumbents have built up significant clearances. Second, payer willingness to reimburse CDS software has improved markedly. Third, generative AI is creating both opportunity and pressure: opportunity to genuinely improve clinical workflows, pressure on incumbents who lack credible AI strategies.
The thesis fits our European healthcare investment platform well.

The European competitive landscape is fragmented across national markets. National scale leaders exist in the UK, Germany, France, and the Nordics, but few players have meaningful pan-European presence. This creates the conditions for a buy-and-build strategy that pairs well with our M&A capabilities.

The category has been under-served by private equity to date. Most scaled European CDS businesses are either bootstrapped, owned by clinical professional bodies, or sit inside larger health IT groups. There is meaningful opportunity for a thoughtful financial sponsor to play a constructive consolidation role.

We see the ideal target as having most of the following characteristics: leadership in at least one national European market; clinical credibility evidenced by professional society endorsement or integration into national clinical guidelines; recurring revenue base of at least EUR 25 million with growth above 15% annually; gross retention above 90%; demonstrated regulatory infrastructure under EU MDR; and a management team genuinely engaged with the AI shift rather than defensive about it.

What is the realistic path to pan-European scale given the inherent fragmentation of European healthcare? Is true cross-border integration achievable, or is the realistic model a portfolio of national champions under common ownership?

European clinical decision support is a structurally attractive software category at an inflection point. We believe it fits our platform well and we recommend Committee endorsement of active sourcing.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Investment thesis — European clinical decision support software

This memo sets out a thematic investment thesis on European clinical decision support ("CDS") software. It is not a transaction memo. We are not yet in dialogue with any specific company. The purpose is to seek Committee endorsement of the thesis itself, which would authorise the team to begin active sourcing and to engage with potential targets at the appropriate level.

The European CDS market is structurally distinct from the US market in several ways. European healthcare is dominated by national payers, which gives CDS products a clearer route to scale once adopted by a national authority. Reimbursement codes for digital health products have improved meaningfully across the major European markets over the past three years. Medical Device Regulation has created higher barriers to entry for serious clinical software, advantaging incumbents who have invested in the regulatory pathway.

We believe the European market is at an inflection point. Three forces are aligning. First, the regulatory pathway under EU MDR is now well-understood and incumbents have built up significant clearances. Second, payer willingness to reimburse CDS software has improved markedly. Third, generative AI is creating both opportunity and pressure: opportunity to genuinely improve clinical workflows, pressure on incumbents who lack credible AI strategies.
The thesis fits our European healthcare investment platform well.

The European competitive landscape is fragmented across national markets. National scale leaders exist in the UK, Germany, France, and the Nordics, but few players have meaningful pan-European presence. This creates the conditions for a buy-and-build strategy that pairs well with our M&A capabilities.

The category has been under-served by private equity to date. Most scaled European CDS businesses are either bootstrapped, owned by clinical professional bodies, or sit inside larger health IT groups. There is meaningful opportunity for a thoughtful financial sponsor to play a constructive consolidation role.

We see the ideal target as having most of the following characteristics: leadership in at least one national European market; clinical credibility evidenced by professional society endorsement or integration into national clinical guidelines; recurring revenue base of at least EUR 25 million with growth above 15% annually; gross retention above 90%; demonstrated regulatory infrastructure under EU MDR; and a management team genuinely engaged with the AI shift rather than defensive about it.

What is the realistic path to pan-European scale given the inherent fragmentation of European healthcare? Is true cross-border integration achievable, or is the realistic model a portfolio of national champions under common ownership?

European clinical decision support is a structurally attractive software category at an inflection point. We believe it fits our platform well and we recommend Committee endorsement of active sourcing.

occurrences.extract: THEMATIC INVESTMENT REVIEW — STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL
To:        Thematic Research Committee
From:      Healthcare Team — Anya Petrov (Member of Management), Felix Mertens (Senior Vice President)
Date:      18 September 2025
Subject:   Investment thesis — European clinical decision support software
PURPOSE OF THIS MEMO

This memo sets out a thematic investment thesis on European clinical decision support ("CDS") software. It is not a transaction memo. We are not yet in dialogue with any specific company. The purpose is to seek Committee endorsement of the thesis itself, which would authorise the team to begin active sourcing and to engage with potential targets at the appropriate level.

Clinical decision support software helps clinicians make better, faster, more consistent treatment decisions at the point of care. The category spans drug interaction checking, diagnostic decision trees, treatment protocol guidance, dosing calculators, and increasingly AI-augmented diagnostic assistance.

The European CDS market is structurally distinct from the US market in several ways. European healthcare is dominated by national payers, which gives CDS products a clearer route to scale once adopted by a national authority. Reimbursement codes for digital health products have improved meaningfully across the major European markets over the past three years. Medical Device Regulation has created higher barriers to entry for serious clinical software, advantaging incumbents who have invested in the regulatory pathway.

We believe the European market is at an inflection point. Three forces are aligning. First, the regulatory pathway under EU MDR is now well-understood and incumbents have built up significant clearances. Second, payer willingness to reimburse CDS software has improved markedly. Third, generative AI is creating both opportunity and pressure: opportunity to genuinely improve clinical workflows, pressure on incumbents who lack credible AI strategies.
The thesis fits our European healthcare investment platform well.

The category produces businesses with strong recurring revenue characteristics, mission-critical product positioning, and high regulatory barriers. Gross retention of 95%+ is typical. EBITDA margins for scaled players can exceed 30%.

The European competitive landscape is fragmented across national markets. National scale leaders exist in the UK, Germany, France, and the Nordics, but few players have meaningful pan-European presence. This creates the conditions for a buy-and-build strategy that pairs well with our M&A capabilities.

The category has been under-served by private equity to date. Most scaled European CDS businesses are either bootstrapped, owned by clinical professional bodies, or sit inside larger health IT groups. There is meaningful opportunity for a thoughtful financial sponsor to play a constructive consolidation role.

We see the ideal target as having most of the following characteristics: leadership in at least one national European market; clinical credibility evidenced by professional society endorsement or integration into national clinical guidelines; recurring revenue base of at least EUR 25 million with growth above 15% annually; gross retention above 90%; demonstrated regulatory infrastructure under EU MDR; and a management team genuinely engaged with the AI shift rather than defensive about it.

We would expect to invest at the platform level with a clear add-on programme. Typical deal size would be in the EUR 100 to 300 million equity ticket range, with an expected hold of five to seven years and a buy-and-build that aims to triple ARR over the hold.
If the Committee endorses this thesis we propose to:

Conduct a structured market mapping exercise over the next eight weeks, working with a specialist healthcare technology advisor. We have approached Mariner Health (a London-based boutique) for an initial scoping conversation.
Begin proactive outreach to a shortlist of approximately 15 to 20 potential targets identified through our preliminary work.

Engage clinical advisors to support our diligence approach on individual opportunities. We have had preliminary conversations with two former chief clinical officers of major UK and German hospital networks.
Plan to return to the Committee within six months with either a specific transaction memo or a refreshed thesis based on what we have learned.
We are not recommending any specific investment at this time. We are seeking endorsement of the thesis and authorisation to invest sourcing time accordingly.

What is the right competitive response to generative AI from a CDS business that has not yet built native AI capability? Is the answer to acquire AI-native challengers, to partner with foundation model providers, or to invest in proprietary models?

How should we think about the role of national health authorities as potential customers, partners, or competitors? In several markets there is active discussion of state-developed clinical decision tools.

What is the realistic path to pan-European scale given the inherent fragmentation of European healthcare? Is true cross-border integration achievable, or is the realistic model a portfolio of national champions under common ownership?
These questions will be sharpened through the sourcing and market mapping work. We would expect to return with clearer perspectives in the next thesis update.

European clinical decision support is a structurally attractive software category at an inflection point. We believe it fits our platform well and we recommend Committee endorsement of active sourcing.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The thesis is clear and the three-forces structure lands well. The strongest passage is the European distinctiveness argument, where the link from fragmented national leadership to a buy-and-build angle that fits our M&A capability is specific and persuasive. The MDR point is also usefully framed as a barrier that benefits incumbents with existing clearances rather than as generic regulatory colour.

The generative AI section is the weakest part and reads as having it both ways: "The opportunity is for products that genuinely improve clinical workflows" sits next to the claim that AI exposes incumbents to challenger risk, without telling the reader which side we think we are investing on. The reimbursement claim that "payer willingness to reimburse digital health products has improved markedly across the major European markets" is doing a lot of work with no evidence attached, and a sentence or two naming specific schemes would make it much harder to push back on. Finally, the close is softer than it needs to be - if a live opportunity is coming, say so plainly and give the committee a sense of timing.

reading.writerFeedback:
The thesis comes across clearly and the structure holds together well. The five value drivers are distinct and quantified, the entry story (bilateral, 18 months, 10-15% discount in exchange for partnership) is a genuine strength and lands with the reader, and the risk section is refreshingly direct rather than defensive. The management transition from Marco Esposito to Elena Conti is handled with the right level of detail, and the unit economics - 22% four-wall margins and 2.4-year payback - do real work in the memo.

A few things are weaker. The UK risk paragraph undersells itself: "We have direct experience of homeware concepts that have failed in the UK market and have mitigated through detailed commercial diligence, a phased rollout, and a recruited UK country manager subject to deal completion" reads as a list of mitigants without telling the IC what actually went wrong in those prior cases or why we think this is different - given UK/Nordics is flagged as the single largest growth contributor, that deserves more. Atelier 73 is introduced as a "fifth value driver" but we get only two numbers (18 stores, younger urban customer) and the claim that it "has potential to become a meaningful growth pillar" - either it carries weight in the plan and should be sized, or it should be demoted to optionality. The wholesale concentration point ("meaningful customer concentration in its top five accounts") is too thin to be useful; a percentage would settle it. Finally, the base case returns are stated but there is no downside case cited alongside the German stress test, which the IC will ask for.

We seek IC approval for an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

We recommend approval of an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity from Halden Group, with the right to syndicate up to EUR 110 million of co-investment, in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. on the terms described.

occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. ("Casa Verde" or "the Company"), a Milan-headquartered premium European homeware and kitchenware retailer and brand owner. The transaction values Casa Verde at an enterprise value of EUR 1.85 billion, representing 12.4x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 149 million.

Casa Verde represents one of the most attractive opportunities our European Consumer team has reviewed in the past five years. The Company combines a strong direct-to-consumer brand with category-leading market share across four European countries, demonstrably strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion that has been deliberately constrained under family ownership.

Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

The Company employs 3,840 people across the four countries, of whom approximately 2,900 are store-based, 540 work in distribution and logistics across three regional centres, 290 work in commercial and merchandising functions, and the remainder are corporate and group functions based in Milan.

First, Casa Verde is a category leader in a structurally attractive sector. Premium homeware in Europe is a EUR 38 billion market growing at 4 to 5 percent annually, with structural tailwinds from continued urbanisation, smaller average household sizes, ongoing premiumisation of the home environment, and the durability of the home-as-sanctuary trend that accelerated through the pandemic. The Company holds an estimated 4.1% share of the addressable European premium market — a meaningful position in a fragmented category where the next largest specialist competitor holds roughly 2.7%.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. This is materially better than premium homeware peers and reflects strong product margins (gross margin of 64.2%), well-managed rent and labour costs, and high inventory turn (4.8 times annually). E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Third, there is a clear and well-defined international expansion runway. The Company has built a successful playbook for entering new markets — typically starting with three to four flagship locations in a top-tier city, building brand awareness through these stores, then expanding the network and rolling out e-commerce in parallel. The playbook has been executed successfully in France (entered 2014, now 32 stores), Spain (entered 2017, now 21 stores), and Germany (entered 2019, now 24 stores). The next logical markets are the UK, the Netherlands, and the Nordic region, none of which have been entered. Our commercial diligence suggests substantial unmet demand for premium homeware in these markets that is currently served by department stores and online aggregators rather than dedicated category specialists.

Fourth, there is meaningful product-side opportunity. The Company's own-brand product penetration has grown from 38% in 2020 to 54% in 2025, supported by investment in the in-house design studio. Each percentage point of own-brand penetration uplift is worth approximately EUR 4 million in gross margin. We see a credible path to 70% own-brand penetration over a five-year hold, contributing approximately 250 basis points of gross margin expansion.

Fifth, the Atelier 73 concept has the potential to become a meaningful third growth pillar. The 18 stores operating today generate average four-wall margins of 18%, slightly below the core Casa Verde concept, but the format is younger, less proven, and at much earlier scale. The format's appeal to a clearly differentiated customer cohort (younger, more design-led, more urban) gives the Company a vehicle to capture share in segments where the core Casa Verde brand does not naturally resonate. We have underwritten conservative growth for Atelier 73 in our base case but see meaningful upside if the concept proves out at scale.

Consumer discretionary exposure. Homeware is a discretionary purchase, and the European consumer environment in 2025 is uneven. Italy and Spain have shown strong like-for-like growth (5% and 6% respectively in 2025); France has been weaker (1.5%); Germany has been actively negative (-2.8%) reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer spending. We have stress-tested our model assuming sustained German weakness through 2027 and the returns remain attractive. A broader European consumer downturn would put pressure on the plan; we are comfortable that the Company's premium positioning and resilient unit economics give meaningful downside protection.

Family transition. The Esposito family has owned Casa Verde for 53 years. Marco Esposito, son of the founder, has served as Chairman and CEO since 2008. He will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close but will remain Chairman for at least three years. The current Chief Operating Officer, Elena Conti, will assume the CEO role. Elena has been with the Company for 17 years, is highly regarded across the management team, and has been involved in every major strategic decision over the past decade. Reference checks have been comprehensive and uniformly positive. We see this transition as well-managed but acknowledge that it represents change.

Real estate exposure. The Company leases 167 of its 184 store locations (the remainder are owned). Lease commitments are EUR 38 million annually with a weighted average remaining term of 7.2 years. Most leases include break clauses at the five-year mark. We have stress-tested our model for the scenario in which 10% of leases are renegotiated upward by 20% at the next break, and the impact on returns is modest. We have not stress-tested for a more severe scenario but flag it as a watch item.

The wider senior team comprises an experienced CFO (Roberto Marchetti, 12 years with the Company), a strong Head of Commercial (Anne-Laure Dubois, 6 years), an excellent Head of E-commerce (Hannah Schmidt, recruited in 2022 from Mytheresa), and the Head of Design and Sourcing (Lucia Marini, 22 years with the Company). The team has very low turnover and exceptional alignment.

Commercial diligence was conducted by Bain & Company over a ten-week period concluding in early January 2026. The Bain report (circulated separately) confirms market positioning, validates the international expansion thesis, and provides detailed competitive mapping. Key conclusions: Casa Verde occupies a defensible premium position with limited direct overlap with mass-market homeware retailers; international expansion potential in the prospective new markets is significant and consistent with the Company's own commercial assessment; the Atelier 73 concept has meaningful upside but is at an early stage of proof.

Financial and tax diligence was conducted by Deloitte. No issues of material consequence. The financial reporting infrastructure is appropriate for the Company's current scale but will require investment to support our expansion ambitions; we have factored this into our planning.

ESG diligence was conducted by ERM. The Company has strong fundamentals on sourcing transparency (a function of the predominantly European supplier base for many product categories), employee practices (employee engagement scores in the top quartile for European retailers), and environmental footprint (well-developed sustainability framework, although Scope 3 emissions reporting requires significant enhancement). We have identified Scope 3 reporting and packaging recycling as priority areas for post-close work.

This is a relatively unusual transaction for our team in that the Company is performing strongly and the value creation plan is a programme of acceleration rather than transformation. The principal risk in such transactions is that operational urgency can be hard to establish; the team is rightly proud of what they have built and may not see the need for change. We have given this risk careful thought.

First, we will work alongside the management team to formalise a strategic roadmap with specific targets, timelines, and accountability mechanisms. The Company does not currently have this kind of structured strategic planning. Elena Conti has indicated strong appetite for it. We see this as foundational.

Second, we will introduce greater performance management discipline, particularly around the international expansion and the digital transformation programmes. The Company has historically operated with a relatively informal management style that has served it well at its current scale but will need to evolve as the Company moves toward a more international and digitally-led future.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

Direct sourcing capability is well-developed for European suppliers but less mature for Asian sourcing, where the Company has historically relied more heavily on trading partner relationships. The new Hanoi office is intended to address this and to increase direct sourcing share in Asia from approximately 35% today to 65% over three years. This is a meaningful contributor to the gross margin expansion thesis.

Total interest expense in year one is expected to be approximately EUR 45 million, well-covered by anticipated cash generation. The Company is expected to be deleveraging from year one onwards, with net debt expected to reduce from EUR 630 million at close to approximately EUR 480 million by end of year three, despite the significant capex programme.

We have stress-tested the financing structure under multiple downside scenarios, including the severe downside case in which European consumer demand contracts by 8% sustained over two years. In this scenario the leverage covenant has approximately 25% headroom and the Company remains free cash flow positive throughout, even with elevated capex.

We seek IC approval for an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. ("Casa Verde" or "the Company"), a Milan-headquartered premium European homeware and kitchenware retailer and brand owner. The transaction values Casa Verde at an enterprise value of EUR 1.85 billion, representing 12.4x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 149 million.

Casa Verde represents one of the most attractive opportunities our European Consumer team has reviewed in the past five years. The Company combines a strong direct-to-consumer brand with category-leading market share across four European countries, demonstrably strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion that has been deliberately constrained under family ownership.

Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

First, Casa Verde is a category leader in a structurally attractive sector. Premium homeware in Europe is a EUR 38 billion market growing at 4 to 5 percent annually, with structural tailwinds from continued urbanisation, smaller average household sizes, ongoing premiumisation of the home environment, and the durability of the home-as-sanctuary trend that accelerated through the pandemic. The Company holds an estimated 4.1% share of the addressable European premium market — a meaningful position in a fragmented category where the next largest specialist competitor holds roughly 2.7%.

Consumer discretionary exposure. Homeware is a discretionary purchase, and the European consumer environment in 2025 is uneven. Italy and Spain have shown strong like-for-like growth (5% and 6% respectively in 2025); France has been weaker (1.5%); Germany has been actively negative (-2.8%) reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer spending. We have stress-tested our model assuming sustained German weakness through 2027 and the returns remain attractive. A broader European consumer downturn would put pressure on the plan; we are comfortable that the Company's premium positioning and resilient unit economics give meaningful downside protection.

ESG diligence was conducted by ERM. The Company has strong fundamentals on sourcing transparency (a function of the predominantly European supplier base for many product categories), employee practices (employee engagement scores in the top quartile for European retailers), and environmental footprint (well-developed sustainability framework, although Scope 3 emissions reporting requires significant enhancement). We have identified Scope 3 reporting and packaging recycling as priority areas for post-close work.

Our base case generates a 2.7x MOIC and 22% gross IRR over a six-year hold. The upside case — assuming international expansion delivers faster than planned and the Atelier 73 concept proves out as a meaningful third growth pillar — generates 3.5x MOIC and 28% gross IRR. The downside case — assuming a sustained European consumer downturn, slower international expansion, and modest multiple compression at exit — generates 1.7x MOIC and 11% gross IRR.

We have stress-tested the downside case extensively. The principal driver of the downside is slower-than-expected international expansion combined with a 200 basis point EBITDA margin compression in the existing business. Under these assumptions returns are modest but positive; we do not see a credible scenario in which the investment produces a loss of capital absent a severe and sustained European consumer recession.
The European premium homeware market is fragmented but evolving. We have mapped the competitive landscape in detail through our commercial diligence.
The remaining EUR 0 million is from minimal cross-border e-commerce sales into other European countries, which represents the principal evidence base for the international expansion thesis.

Casa Verde sources approximately 56% of its product (by value) from European suppliers, principally in Italy, Portugal, France, and Germany. The remaining 44% is sourced from Asia, primarily from a network of 38 long-standing suppliers in China and Vietnam, managed through the sourcing office in Porto and (in due course) the new office in Hanoi.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

Direct sourcing capability is well-developed for European suppliers but less mature for Asian sourcing, where the Company has historically relied more heavily on trading partner relationships. The new Hanoi office is intended to address this and to increase direct sourcing share in Asia from approximately 35% today to 65% over three years. This is a meaningful contributor to the gross margin expansion thesis.

We have stress-tested the financing structure under multiple downside scenarios, including the severe downside case in which European consumer demand contracts by 8% sustained over two years. In this scenario the leverage covenant has approximately 25% headroom and the Company remains free cash flow positive throughout, even with elevated capex.

Casa Verde represents an outstanding opportunity to acquire a high-quality European consumer business with category leadership, strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion. The transaction is being completed on a bilaterally negotiated basis with a long-standing family seller at attractive economics. The management team is strong, the value creation plan is well-defined, and the financing structure is appropriately conservative.

Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

The Company employs 3,840 people across the four countries, of whom approximately 2,900 are store-based, 540 work in distribution and logistics across three regional centres, 290 work in commercial and merchandising functions, and the remainder are corporate and group functions based in Milan.

First, Casa Verde is a category leader in a structurally attractive sector. Premium homeware in Europe is a EUR 38 billion market growing at 4 to 5 percent annually, with structural tailwinds from continued urbanisation, smaller average household sizes, ongoing premiumisation of the home environment, and the durability of the home-as-sanctuary trend that accelerated through the pandemic. The Company holds an estimated 4.1% share of the addressable European premium market — a meaningful position in a fragmented category where the next largest specialist competitor holds roughly 2.7%.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. This is materially better than premium homeware peers and reflects strong product margins (gross margin of 64.2%), well-managed rent and labour costs, and high inventory turn (4.8 times annually). E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Third, there is a clear and well-defined international expansion runway. The Company has built a successful playbook for entering new markets — typically starting with three to four flagship locations in a top-tier city, building brand awareness through these stores, then expanding the network and rolling out e-commerce in parallel. The playbook has been executed successfully in France (entered 2014, now 32 stores), Spain (entered 2017, now 21 stores), and Germany (entered 2019, now 24 stores). The next logical markets are the UK, the Netherlands, and the Nordic region, none of which have been entered. Our commercial diligence suggests substantial unmet demand for premium homeware in these markets that is currently served by department stores and online aggregators rather than dedicated category specialists.

Fourth, there is meaningful product-side opportunity. The Company's own-brand product penetration has grown from 38% in 2020 to 54% in 2025, supported by investment in the in-house design studio. Each percentage point of own-brand penetration uplift is worth approximately EUR 4 million in gross margin. We see a credible path to 70% own-brand penetration over a five-year hold, contributing approximately 250 basis points of gross margin expansion.

Fifth, the Atelier 73 concept has the potential to become a meaningful third growth pillar. The 18 stores operating today generate average four-wall margins of 18%, slightly below the core Casa Verde concept, but the format is younger, less proven, and at much earlier scale. The format's appeal to a clearly differentiated customer cohort (younger, more design-led, more urban) gives the Company a vehicle to capture share in segments where the core Casa Verde brand does not naturally resonate. We have underwritten conservative growth for Atelier 73 in our base case but see meaningful upside if the concept proves out at scale.

Consumer discretionary exposure. Homeware is a discretionary purchase, and the European consumer environment in 2025 is uneven. Italy and Spain have shown strong like-for-like growth (5% and 6% respectively in 2025); France has been weaker (1.5%); Germany has been actively negative (-2.8%) reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer spending. We have stress-tested our model assuming sustained German weakness through 2027 and the returns remain attractive. A broader European consumer downturn would put pressure on the plan; we are comfortable that the Company's premium positioning and resilient unit economics give meaningful downside protection.

Family transition. The Esposito family has owned Casa Verde for 53 years. Marco Esposito, son of the founder, has served as Chairman and CEO since 2008. He will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close but will remain Chairman for at least three years. The current Chief Operating Officer, Elena Conti, will assume the CEO role. Elena has been with the Company for 17 years, is highly regarded across the management team, and has been involved in every major strategic decision over the past decade. Reference checks have been comprehensive and uniformly positive. We see this transition as well-managed but acknowledge that it represents change.

Real estate exposure. The Company leases 167 of its 184 store locations (the remainder are owned). Lease commitments are EUR 38 million annually with a weighted average remaining term of 7.2 years. Most leases include break clauses at the five-year mark. We have stress-tested our model for the scenario in which 10% of leases are renegotiated upward by 20% at the next break, and the impact on returns is modest. We have not stress-tested for a more severe scenario but flag it as a watch item.

The wider senior team comprises an experienced CFO (Roberto Marchetti, 12 years with the Company), a strong Head of Commercial (Anne-Laure Dubois, 6 years), an excellent Head of E-commerce (Hannah Schmidt, recruited in 2022 from Mytheresa), and the Head of Design and Sourcing (Lucia Marini, 22 years with the Company). The team has very low turnover and exceptional alignment.

Commercial diligence was conducted by Bain & Company over a ten-week period concluding in early January 2026. The Bain report (circulated separately) confirms market positioning, validates the international expansion thesis, and provides detailed competitive mapping. Key conclusions: Casa Verde occupies a defensible premium position with limited direct overlap with mass-market homeware retailers; international expansion potential in the prospective new markets is significant and consistent with the Company's own commercial assessment; the Atelier 73 concept has meaningful upside but is at an early stage of proof.

Financial and tax diligence was conducted by Deloitte. No issues of material consequence. The financial reporting infrastructure is appropriate for the Company's current scale but will require investment to support our expansion ambitions; we have factored this into our planning.

ESG diligence was conducted by ERM. The Company has strong fundamentals on sourcing transparency (a function of the predominantly European supplier base for many product categories), employee practices (employee engagement scores in the top quartile for European retailers), and environmental footprint (well-developed sustainability framework, although Scope 3 emissions reporting requires significant enhancement). We have identified Scope 3 reporting and packaging recycling as priority areas for post-close work.

This is a relatively unusual transaction for our team in that the Company is performing strongly and the value creation plan is a programme of acceleration rather than transformation. The principal risk in such transactions is that operational urgency can be hard to establish; the team is rightly proud of what they have built and may not see the need for change. We have given this risk careful thought.

First, we will work alongside the management team to formalise a strategic roadmap with specific targets, timelines, and accountability mechanisms. The Company does not currently have this kind of structured strategic planning. Elena Conti has indicated strong appetite for it. We see this as foundational.

Second, we will introduce greater performance management discipline, particularly around the international expansion and the digital transformation programmes. The Company has historically operated with a relatively informal management style that has served it well at its current scale but will need to evolve as the Company moves toward a more international and digitally-led future.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

Direct sourcing capability is well-developed for European suppliers but less mature for Asian sourcing, where the Company has historically relied more heavily on trading partner relationships. The new Hanoi office is intended to address this and to increase direct sourcing share in Asia from approximately 35% today to 65% over three years. This is a meaningful contributor to the gross margin expansion thesis.

Total interest expense in year one is expected to be approximately EUR 45 million, well-covered by anticipated cash generation. The Company is expected to be deleveraging from year one onwards, with net debt expected to reduce from EUR 630 million at close to approximately EUR 480 million by end of year three, despite the significant capex programme.

We have stress-tested the financing structure under multiple downside scenarios, including the severe downside case in which European consumer demand contracts by 8% sustained over two years. In this scenario the leverage covenant has approximately 25% headroom and the Company remains free cash flow positive throughout, even with elevated capex.

Total group revenue in the financial year ended 31 December 2025 was EUR 612 million, with EBITDA of EUR 149 million representing a margin of 24.3%. Revenue has grown at a compound annual rate of 11.4% since 2020, with EBITDA margins expanding by approximately 380 basis points over the same period.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Our base case envisages revenue growth from EUR 612 million in 2025 to approximately EUR 1.04 billion in 2031, a compound annual growth rate of 9.2%. EBITDA is expected to grow from EUR 149 million to approximately EUR 295 million over the same period, with margins expanding modestly from 24.3% to 28.4%.

Total leverage at close is 4.3x trailing EBITDA, which we view as appropriately conservative given the consumer discretionary exposure. Goldman Sachs is leading the debt financing process and has provided a fully underwritten commitment letter.

Multiple expansion is not assumed in the base case. We underwrite an exit at 12.0x EBITDA, broadly in line with the entry multiple. The upside case assumes 13.0x at exit, reflecting the higher-growth, more international, more diversified platform that Casa Verde should become.

We have stress-tested the downside case extensively. The principal driver of the downside is slower-than-expected international expansion combined with a 200 basis point EBITDA margin compression in the existing business. Under these assumptions returns are modest but positive; we do not see a credible scenario in which the investment produces a loss of capital absent a severe and sustained European consumer recession.

In e-commerce, Casa Verde competes with both pure-plays (Westwing, Mytheresa's home business, Made.com prior to its administration) and with the online channels of physical retailers. Casa Verde's e-commerce performance — 31% mix, 19% EBITDA margin — is notably stronger than category benchmarks, reflecting both the strength of the brand and the disciplined approach to digital pricing.
Our base case underwrites the following specific contribution to EBITDA growth over the hold.

International expansion (UK, Netherlands, Nordics): EUR 42 million of incremental EBITDA by 2031, comprising EUR 22 million from the UK programme (28 stores by 2031, average mature-store contribution of EUR 800k), EUR 9 million from the Netherlands (10 stores, EUR 900k average), and EUR 11 million from the Nordics (14 stores across Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, average EUR 800k).

Own-brand penetration uplift: EUR 28 million of incremental EBITDA, driven by 16 percentage points of own-brand mix improvement (from 54% to 70%) on a revenue base that will be EUR 1.04 billion by 2031, with each percentage point worth approximately EUR 1.75 million at scale.

Direct sourcing expansion: EUR 12 million of incremental EBITDA from the Asian direct sourcing programme, reflecting approximately 280 basis points of gross margin improvement on the approximately EUR 460 million of Asian-sourced revenue at exit.
Like-for-like growth in existing markets: EUR 18 million of incremental EBITDA, reflecting modest revenue growth in the existing 184-store base and modest operating leverage.
Atelier 73 expansion: EUR 14 million of incremental EBITDA, assuming the format expands to 42 stores by 2031 (from 18 today) at a mature contribution profile consistent with current performance.
E-commerce platform investment: EUR 8 million of incremental EBITDA, reflecting both renewed channel growth and improved conversion economics following the platform replacement.

Cost discipline and operating leverage: EUR 24 million of incremental EBITDA from the natural operating leverage of the broader cost base on incremental revenue, partially offset by ongoing investment in central capabilities.
Total incremental EBITDA: EUR 146 million, taking the base of EUR 149 million to EUR 295 million by 2031.
