occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. ("Casa Verde" or "the Company"), a Milan-headquartered premium European homeware and kitchenware retailer and brand owner. The transaction values Casa Verde at an enterprise value of EUR 1.85 billion, representing 12.4x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 149 million.

Casa Verde represents one of the most attractive opportunities our European Consumer team has reviewed in the past five years. The Company combines a strong direct-to-consumer brand with category-leading market share across four European countries, demonstrably strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion that has been deliberately constrained under family ownership.

Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

The Company employs 3,840 people across the four countries, of whom approximately 2,900 are store-based, 540 work in distribution and logistics across three regional centres, 290 work in commercial and merchandising functions, and the remainder are corporate and group functions based in Milan.

First, Casa Verde is a category leader in a structurally attractive sector. Premium homeware in Europe is a EUR 38 billion market growing at 4 to 5 percent annually, with structural tailwinds from continued urbanisation, smaller average household sizes, ongoing premiumisation of the home environment, and the durability of the home-as-sanctuary trend that accelerated through the pandemic. The Company holds an estimated 4.1% share of the addressable European premium market — a meaningful position in a fragmented category where the next largest specialist competitor holds roughly 2.7%.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. This is materially better than premium homeware peers and reflects strong product margins (gross margin of 64.2%), well-managed rent and labour costs, and high inventory turn (4.8 times annually). E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Third, there is a clear and well-defined international expansion runway. The Company has built a successful playbook for entering new markets — typically starting with three to four flagship locations in a top-tier city, building brand awareness through these stores, then expanding the network and rolling out e-commerce in parallel. The playbook has been executed successfully in France (entered 2014, now 32 stores), Spain (entered 2017, now 21 stores), and Germany (entered 2019, now 24 stores). The next logical markets are the UK, the Netherlands, and the Nordic region, none of which have been entered. Our commercial diligence suggests substantial unmet demand for premium homeware in these markets that is currently served by department stores and online aggregators rather than dedicated category specialists.

Fourth, there is meaningful product-side opportunity. The Company's own-brand product penetration has grown from 38% in 2020 to 54% in 2025, supported by investment in the in-house design studio. Each percentage point of own-brand penetration uplift is worth approximately EUR 4 million in gross margin. We see a credible path to 70% own-brand penetration over a five-year hold, contributing approximately 250 basis points of gross margin expansion.

Fifth, the Atelier 73 concept has the potential to become a meaningful third growth pillar. The 18 stores operating today generate average four-wall margins of 18%, slightly below the core Casa Verde concept, but the format is younger, less proven, and at much earlier scale. The format's appeal to a clearly differentiated customer cohort (younger, more design-led, more urban) gives the Company a vehicle to capture share in segments where the core Casa Verde brand does not naturally resonate. We have underwritten conservative growth for Atelier 73 in our base case but see meaningful upside if the concept proves out at scale.

Consumer discretionary exposure. Homeware is a discretionary purchase, and the European consumer environment in 2025 is uneven. Italy and Spain have shown strong like-for-like growth (5% and 6% respectively in 2025); France has been weaker (1.5%); Germany has been actively negative (-2.8%) reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer spending. We have stress-tested our model assuming sustained German weakness through 2027 and the returns remain attractive. A broader European consumer downturn would put pressure on the plan; we are comfortable that the Company's premium positioning and resilient unit economics give meaningful downside protection.

Family transition. The Esposito family has owned Casa Verde for 53 years. Marco Esposito, son of the founder, has served as Chairman and CEO since 2008. He will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close but will remain Chairman for at least three years. The current Chief Operating Officer, Elena Conti, will assume the CEO role. Elena has been with the Company for 17 years, is highly regarded across the management team, and has been involved in every major strategic decision over the past decade. Reference checks have been comprehensive and uniformly positive. We see this transition as well-managed but acknowledge that it represents change.

Real estate exposure. The Company leases 167 of its 184 store locations (the remainder are owned). Lease commitments are EUR 38 million annually with a weighted average remaining term of 7.2 years. Most leases include break clauses at the five-year mark. We have stress-tested our model for the scenario in which 10% of leases are renegotiated upward by 20% at the next break, and the impact on returns is modest. We have not stress-tested for a more severe scenario but flag it as a watch item.

The wider senior team comprises an experienced CFO (Roberto Marchetti, 12 years with the Company), a strong Head of Commercial (Anne-Laure Dubois, 6 years), an excellent Head of E-commerce (Hannah Schmidt, recruited in 2022 from Mytheresa), and the Head of Design and Sourcing (Lucia Marini, 22 years with the Company). The team has very low turnover and exceptional alignment.

Commercial diligence was conducted by Bain & Company over a ten-week period concluding in early January 2026. The Bain report (circulated separately) confirms market positioning, validates the international expansion thesis, and provides detailed competitive mapping. Key conclusions: Casa Verde occupies a defensible premium position with limited direct overlap with mass-market homeware retailers; international expansion potential in the prospective new markets is significant and consistent with the Company's own commercial assessment; the Atelier 73 concept has meaningful upside but is at an early stage of proof.

Financial and tax diligence was conducted by Deloitte. No issues of material consequence. The financial reporting infrastructure is appropriate for the Company's current scale but will require investment to support our expansion ambitions; we have factored this into our planning.

ESG diligence was conducted by ERM. The Company has strong fundamentals on sourcing transparency (a function of the predominantly European supplier base for many product categories), employee practices (employee engagement scores in the top quartile for European retailers), and environmental footprint (well-developed sustainability framework, although Scope 3 emissions reporting requires significant enhancement). We have identified Scope 3 reporting and packaging recycling as priority areas for post-close work.

This is a relatively unusual transaction for our team in that the Company is performing strongly and the value creation plan is a programme of acceleration rather than transformation. The principal risk in such transactions is that operational urgency can be hard to establish; the team is rightly proud of what they have built and may not see the need for change. We have given this risk careful thought.

First, we will work alongside the management team to formalise a strategic roadmap with specific targets, timelines, and accountability mechanisms. The Company does not currently have this kind of structured strategic planning. Elena Conti has indicated strong appetite for it. We see this as foundational.

Second, we will introduce greater performance management discipline, particularly around the international expansion and the digital transformation programmes. The Company has historically operated with a relatively informal management style that has served it well at its current scale but will need to evolve as the Company moves toward a more international and digitally-led future.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

Direct sourcing capability is well-developed for European suppliers but less mature for Asian sourcing, where the Company has historically relied more heavily on trading partner relationships. The new Hanoi office is intended to address this and to increase direct sourcing share in Asia from approximately 35% today to 65% over three years. This is a meaningful contributor to the gross margin expansion thesis.

Total interest expense in year one is expected to be approximately EUR 45 million, well-covered by anticipated cash generation. The Company is expected to be deleveraging from year one onwards, with net debt expected to reduce from EUR 630 million at close to approximately EUR 480 million by end of year three, despite the significant capex programme.

We have stress-tested the financing structure under multiple downside scenarios, including the severe downside case in which European consumer demand contracts by 8% sustained over two years. In this scenario the leverage covenant has approximately 25% headroom and the Company remains free cash flow positive throughout, even with elevated capex.

sentences.text: Marco Esposito will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close, with Elena Conti (current COO and 17-year company veteran) becoming CEO.

occurrences.extract: Family transition. The Esposito family has owned Casa Verde for 53 years. Marco Esposito, son of the founder, has served as Chairman and CEO since 2008. He will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close but will remain Chairman for at least three years. The current Chief Operating Officer, Elena Conti, will assume the CEO role. Elena has been with the Company for 17 years, is highly regarded across the management team, and has been involved in every major strategic decision over the past decade. Reference checks have been comprehensive and uniformly positive. We see this transition as well-managed but acknowledge that it represents change.

The Esposito family will retain a 10% interest. Management will retain 6%. Halden Group and co-investors will hold 84% in aggregate. We have negotiated majority Halden Group board control (3 of 5 seats) with the Esposito family retaining a board seat for the duration of Marco Esposito's chairmanship.

The management team is strong. Elena Conti (incoming CEO) is well-known to our team — we have had three independent diligence conversations with her over the past four months and the consistency and depth of her thinking across operating, financial, and strategic dimensions has been impressive. Marco Esposito (continuing Chairman) has run the business for 18 years with a steady hand and continues to bring genuine strategic value through customer relationships and industry credibility.

The board will be composed of five members: three Halden Group representatives (Charlotte Verstappen as Chair of the Board post Marco Esposito's transition, plus two additional team members), Marco Esposito (continuing Chairman in the interim period, transitioning to senior advisor), and Elena Conti (incoming CEO). We have agreed standard reserved matters, with particular attention to capital allocation decisions above defined thresholds and to senior hiring decisions.

occurrences.extract: Casa Verde represents one of the most attractive opportunities our European Consumer team has reviewed in the past five years. The Company combines a strong direct-to-consumer brand with category-leading market share across four European countries, demonstrably strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion that has been deliberately constrained under family ownership.
Our thesis rests on five pillars.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. This is materially better than premium homeware peers and reflects strong product margins (gross margin of 64.2%), well-managed rent and labour costs, and high inventory turn (4.8 times annually). E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Fourth, there is meaningful product-side opportunity. The Company's own-brand product penetration has grown from 38% in 2020 to 54% in 2025, supported by investment in the in-house design studio. Each percentage point of own-brand penetration uplift is worth approximately EUR 4 million in gross margin. We see a credible path to 70% own-brand penetration over a five-year hold, contributing approximately 250 basis points of gross margin expansion.
We have identified five principal risks.

The wholesale channel — accounting for 14% of revenue — has meaningful customer concentration, with the top five wholesale accounts representing 40% of channel revenue. We have reviewed each of these relationships in diligence and they are stable, but we note the dependency.

Germany contributes EUR 90 million of revenue (15% of group). The 24 German stores are spread more thinly across Hamburg (5), Munich (5), Berlin (4), Frankfurt (3), and other cities. Like-for-like growth in Germany was -2.8% in 2025, reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer discretionary spending. The German e-commerce business contributes 35% of country revenue, the highest single-country share in the group, reflecting partly the more dispersed store footprint.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

occurrences.extract: The retail network is organised under three brand banners. Casa Verde itself accounts for 142 of the stores and approximately 78% of revenue, focused on the premium end of the everyday homeware market — ceramics, glassware, kitchen tools, table linens, and decorative objects. The Bellucci banner, acquired by Casa Verde in 2018, operates 24 stores at a higher price point with a stronger fashion-led aesthetic. The Atelier 73 banner — relaunched in 2022 — operates 18 small-format stores targeting younger urban customers with a curated, design-led assortment.

Fifth, the Atelier 73 concept has the potential to become a meaningful third growth pillar. The 18 stores operating today generate average four-wall margins of 18%, slightly below the core Casa Verde concept, but the format is younger, less proven, and at much earlier scale. The format's appeal to a clearly differentiated customer cohort (younger, more design-led, more urban) gives the Company a vehicle to capture share in segments where the core Casa Verde brand does not naturally resonate. We have underwritten conservative growth for Atelier 73 in our base case but see meaningful upside if the concept proves out at scale.

E-commerce and digital. The current e-commerce contribution of 31% of group revenue is strong but has plateaued over the past 18 months. We will invest in a refreshed digital platform (replacement of the current Salesforce Commerce Cloud implementation with a more flexible composable architecture), in expanded personalisation capabilities, and in a CRM-led approach to repeat customer engagement. The investment is approximately EUR 22 million across the hold and is expected to support continued mix shift toward e-commerce at improved margins.

The transaction has been negotiated bilaterally with the family over an 18-month period. We have not been through a competitive process, which has been deliberate on both sides. The agreed enterprise value of EUR 1.85 billion represents a discount of approximately 10 to 15 percent to what we estimate the asset would attract in a fully competitive auction, reflecting the family's stated preference for a partner over the highest price.

The management team is strong. Elena Conti (incoming CEO) is well-known to our team — we have had three independent diligence conversations with her over the past four months and the consistency and depth of her thinking across operating, financial, and strategic dimensions has been impressive. Marco Esposito (continuing Chairman) has run the business for 18 years with a steady hand and continues to bring genuine strategic value through customer relationships and industry credibility.

The e-commerce channel generates EUR 190 million of revenue in 2025, with gross margins of 61.8% (modestly lower than retail due to fulfilment costs) and contribution margins of 19.4%. The channel has grown at 18% annually since 2020 but has plateaued over the past 18 months, reflecting both maturation of the existing customer base and constraints on the current technology platform. The platform replacement programme is expected to unlock renewed growth.

The first eighteen months will focus on transitioning the existing Vietnamese supplier relationships from agent-mediated to direct, conducting a structured supplier audit programme, and beginning to consolidate the supplier base. We expect to reduce the active Asian supplier count from approximately 38 today to a focused group of 20 to 25 over the three-year period, while increasing direct contracting share. This consolidation will deliver both procurement savings and improved quality consistency.
Atelier 73 expansion: EUR 14 million of incremental EBITDA, assuming the format expands to 42 stores by 2031 (from 18 today) at a mature contribution profile consistent with current performance.

sentences.text: In summary, the Company offers exceptional category positioning, defensible unit economics, and a clear international growth runway.

occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of up to EUR 720 million of equity in the acquisition of Casa Verde Group S.p.A. ("Casa Verde" or "the Company"), a Milan-headquartered premium European homeware and kitchenware retailer and brand owner. The transaction values Casa Verde at an enterprise value of EUR 1.85 billion, representing 12.4x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 149 million.

Casa Verde represents one of the most attractive opportunities our European Consumer team has reviewed in the past five years. The Company combines a strong direct-to-consumer brand with category-leading market share across four European countries, demonstrably strong unit economics, and a clear runway for international expansion that has been deliberately constrained under family ownership.

Casa Verde was founded in 1973 by Giovanni Esposito as a single homewares shop in Milan. The Company has grown organically and through measured acquisitions into a pan-European premium homeware and kitchenware specialist with operations across Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The Company currently operates 184 retail stores, an e-commerce platform that generates 31% of group revenue, and a wholesale business that supplies independent design-led homeware retailers across Europe.

The Company employs 3,840 people across the four countries, of whom approximately 2,900 are store-based, 540 work in distribution and logistics across three regional centres, 290 work in commercial and merchandising functions, and the remainder are corporate and group functions based in Milan.

First, Casa Verde is a category leader in a structurally attractive sector. Premium homeware in Europe is a EUR 38 billion market growing at 4 to 5 percent annually, with structural tailwinds from continued urbanisation, smaller average household sizes, ongoing premiumisation of the home environment, and the durability of the home-as-sanctuary trend that accelerated through the pandemic. The Company holds an estimated 4.1% share of the addressable European premium market — a meaningful position in a fragmented category where the next largest specialist competitor holds roughly 2.7%.

Second, the unit economics of Casa Verde stores are exceptional. The Company's average four-wall store EBITDA margin is 22%, with payback on new store openings averaging 2.4 years. This is materially better than premium homeware peers and reflects strong product margins (gross margin of 64.2%), well-managed rent and labour costs, and high inventory turn (4.8 times annually). E-commerce contributes an EBITDA margin of 19%, which is unusually strong for the category and reflects the Company's deliberate strategy of charging full price online rather than discounting to compete on price.

Third, there is a clear and well-defined international expansion runway. The Company has built a successful playbook for entering new markets — typically starting with three to four flagship locations in a top-tier city, building brand awareness through these stores, then expanding the network and rolling out e-commerce in parallel. The playbook has been executed successfully in France (entered 2014, now 32 stores), Spain (entered 2017, now 21 stores), and Germany (entered 2019, now 24 stores). The next logical markets are the UK, the Netherlands, and the Nordic region, none of which have been entered. Our commercial diligence suggests substantial unmet demand for premium homeware in these markets that is currently served by department stores and online aggregators rather than dedicated category specialists.

Fourth, there is meaningful product-side opportunity. The Company's own-brand product penetration has grown from 38% in 2020 to 54% in 2025, supported by investment in the in-house design studio. Each percentage point of own-brand penetration uplift is worth approximately EUR 4 million in gross margin. We see a credible path to 70% own-brand penetration over a five-year hold, contributing approximately 250 basis points of gross margin expansion.

Fifth, the Atelier 73 concept has the potential to become a meaningful third growth pillar. The 18 stores operating today generate average four-wall margins of 18%, slightly below the core Casa Verde concept, but the format is younger, less proven, and at much earlier scale. The format's appeal to a clearly differentiated customer cohort (younger, more design-led, more urban) gives the Company a vehicle to capture share in segments where the core Casa Verde brand does not naturally resonate. We have underwritten conservative growth for Atelier 73 in our base case but see meaningful upside if the concept proves out at scale.

Consumer discretionary exposure. Homeware is a discretionary purchase, and the European consumer environment in 2025 is uneven. Italy and Spain have shown strong like-for-like growth (5% and 6% respectively in 2025); France has been weaker (1.5%); Germany has been actively negative (-2.8%) reflecting the broader weakness in German consumer spending. We have stress-tested our model assuming sustained German weakness through 2027 and the returns remain attractive. A broader European consumer downturn would put pressure on the plan; we are comfortable that the Company's premium positioning and resilient unit economics give meaningful downside protection.

Family transition. The Esposito family has owned Casa Verde for 53 years. Marco Esposito, son of the founder, has served as Chairman and CEO since 2008. He will step back from day-to-day responsibilities post-close but will remain Chairman for at least three years. The current Chief Operating Officer, Elena Conti, will assume the CEO role. Elena has been with the Company for 17 years, is highly regarded across the management team, and has been involved in every major strategic decision over the past decade. Reference checks have been comprehensive and uniformly positive. We see this transition as well-managed but acknowledge that it represents change.

Real estate exposure. The Company leases 167 of its 184 store locations (the remainder are owned). Lease commitments are EUR 38 million annually with a weighted average remaining term of 7.2 years. Most leases include break clauses at the five-year mark. We have stress-tested our model for the scenario in which 10% of leases are renegotiated upward by 20% at the next break, and the impact on returns is modest. We have not stress-tested for a more severe scenario but flag it as a watch item.

The wider senior team comprises an experienced CFO (Roberto Marchetti, 12 years with the Company), a strong Head of Commercial (Anne-Laure Dubois, 6 years), an excellent Head of E-commerce (Hannah Schmidt, recruited in 2022 from Mytheresa), and the Head of Design and Sourcing (Lucia Marini, 22 years with the Company). The team has very low turnover and exceptional alignment.

Commercial diligence was conducted by Bain & Company over a ten-week period concluding in early January 2026. The Bain report (circulated separately) confirms market positioning, validates the international expansion thesis, and provides detailed competitive mapping. Key conclusions: Casa Verde occupies a defensible premium position with limited direct overlap with mass-market homeware retailers; international expansion potential in the prospective new markets is significant and consistent with the Company's own commercial assessment; the Atelier 73 concept has meaningful upside but is at an early stage of proof.

Financial and tax diligence was conducted by Deloitte. No issues of material consequence. The financial reporting infrastructure is appropriate for the Company's current scale but will require investment to support our expansion ambitions; we have factored this into our planning.

ESG diligence was conducted by ERM. The Company has strong fundamentals on sourcing transparency (a function of the predominantly European supplier base for many product categories), employee practices (employee engagement scores in the top quartile for European retailers), and environmental footprint (well-developed sustainability framework, although Scope 3 emissions reporting requires significant enhancement). We have identified Scope 3 reporting and packaging recycling as priority areas for post-close work.

This is a relatively unusual transaction for our team in that the Company is performing strongly and the value creation plan is a programme of acceleration rather than transformation. The principal risk in such transactions is that operational urgency can be hard to establish; the team is rightly proud of what they have built and may not see the need for change. We have given this risk careful thought.

First, we will work alongside the management team to formalise a strategic roadmap with specific targets, timelines, and accountability mechanisms. The Company does not currently have this kind of structured strategic planning. Elena Conti has indicated strong appetite for it. We see this as foundational.

Second, we will introduce greater performance management discipline, particularly around the international expansion and the digital transformation programmes. The Company has historically operated with a relatively informal management style that has served it well at its current scale but will need to evolve as the Company moves toward a more international and digitally-led future.

The European supplier base provides differentiation in product quality and design (particularly for ceramics, glassware, and table linens) and is a meaningful contributor to the premium positioning. The Asian supplier base provides cost discipline on more commoditised product categories. The Company has been gradually shifting the European share upward over the past five years; it was 48% in 2020.

Direct sourcing capability is well-developed for European suppliers but less mature for Asian sourcing, where the Company has historically relied more heavily on trading partner relationships. The new Hanoi office is intended to address this and to increase direct sourcing share in Asia from approximately 35% today to 65% over three years. This is a meaningful contributor to the gross margin expansion thesis.

Total interest expense in year one is expected to be approximately EUR 45 million, well-covered by anticipated cash generation. The Company is expected to be deleveraging from year one onwards, with net debt expected to reduce from EUR 630 million at close to approximately EUR 480 million by end of year three, despite the significant capex programme.

We have stress-tested the financing structure under multiple downside scenarios, including the severe downside case in which European consumer demand contracts by 8% sustained over two years. In this scenario the leverage covenant has approximately 25% headroom and the Company remains free cash flow positive throughout, even with elevated capex.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The thesis comes across clearly and the structure holds together well. The five value drivers are distinct and quantified, the entry story (bilateral, 18 months, 10-15% discount in exchange for partnership) is a genuine strength and lands with the reader, and the risk section is refreshingly direct rather than defensive. The management transition from Marco Esposito to Elena Conti is handled with the right level of detail, and the unit economics - 22% four-wall margins and 2.4-year payback - do real work in the memo.

A few things are weaker. The UK risk paragraph undersells itself: "We have direct experience of homeware concepts that have failed in the UK market and have mitigated through detailed commercial diligence, a phased rollout, and a recruited UK country manager subject to deal completion" reads as a list of mitigants without telling the IC what actually went wrong in those prior cases or why we think this is different - given UK/Nordics is flagged as the single largest growth contributor, that deserves more. Atelier 73 is introduced as a "fifth value driver" but we get only two numbers (18 stores, younger urban customer) and the claim that it "has potential to become a meaningful growth pillar" - either it carries weight in the plan and should be sized, or it should be demoted to optionality. The wholesale concentration point ("meaningful customer concentration in its top five accounts") is too thin to be useful; a percentage would settle it. Finally, the base case returns are stated but there is no downside case cited alongside the German stress test, which the IC will ask for.

reading.writerFeedback:
The memo lands the essentials cleanly and the thesis hangs together. The unit economics are presented in the right order, the channel mix gives a quick read of the business model, and the risk section is honest rather than decorative - calling out that payback has drifted from 3.8 months to 5.2 months is exactly the kind of disclosure the IC will want to see up front. The founder-dependency flag on Sarah Whitmore is also well placed given how the brand is positioned.

That said, the thesis section is doing too much work in one sentence and glosses the hardest question. We say there is 'a clear international runway in France, Italy, Spain, and selectively in the US over a five-year hold,' but we give the reader nothing on sequencing, local CAC assumptions, or why a UK DTC brand should travel - this is the load-bearing assumption behind getting from EUR 64 million to EUR 195 million and it deserves its own paragraph. Relatedly, the base case jump to 2.9x and 24% IRR is asserted without a bridge; even a two-line walk (growth, margin, exit multiple) would make it defensible. I would also tighten the regulatory risk line, which currently trails off vaguely - name the specific claims regimes we are worried about.

sentences.text: Bloom Nutrition is a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition brand offering an evidence-based supplement range across four primary categories: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Caraway — Proposed acquisition of Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.

Bloom was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists. The Company operates in the premium women's health and nutrition category, offering a focused range of evidence-based supplement products targeting four primary use cases: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

Bloom operates with a small but capable team of 67 people, headquartered in London with a 12-person team in Berlin focused on the DACH market. The Company has a clinical advisory board of seven specialists across endocrinology, nutrition, and women's health, which contributes to both product development and to the brand's clinical credibility.

Regulatory risk in women's health is real. Several of Bloom's products make claims around hormonal support and pregnancy wellness that are subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny across European markets. The Company has invested appropriately in regulatory affairs and has a clean track record, but the regulatory environment for nutrition claims is becoming more demanding.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Caraway — Proposed acquisition of Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.

The multiple appears full but reflects Bloom's growth profile (47% revenue CAGR over the past three years), premium positioning, and the strategic optionality created by a well-defined and proven brand platform.

Bloom was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists. The Company operates in the premium women's health and nutrition category, offering a focused range of evidence-based supplement products targeting four primary use cases: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

The product range comprises 24 SKUs, all formulated in-house, manufactured under contract by GMP-certified European facilities, and sold direct-to-consumer through Bloom's own website and Amazon, alongside a select wholesale presence in premium retailers including Selfridges, Le Bon Marché, KaDeWe, and Sephora.

Bloom operates with a small but capable team of 67 people, headquartered in London with a 12-person team in Berlin focused on the DACH market. The Company has a clinical advisory board of seven specialists across endocrinology, nutrition, and women's health, which contributes to both product development and to the brand's clinical credibility.

Premium women's health is a structurally attractive emerging category. Women's health has been historically under-served by both mainstream and premium consumer health brands. The category is growing at approximately 14% annually in Europe, with significantly faster growth in dedicated direct-to-consumer brands. Bloom is well-positioned within this category as a clinically-credible, premium-positioned, multi-product brand.

Bloom has built a defensible position in a category where most competitors are either single-product brands (limiting customer lifetime value) or insufficiently differentiated. The Company's clinical advisory board, in-house formulation capability, and disciplined product development cadence (typically two new product launches per year) create meaningful competitive moats.

International expansion runway is significant. Bloom is strong in the UK and increasingly strong in DACH, but underdeveloped in France, Italy, and Spain. The brand has demonstrable cross-border appeal — DACH revenue has grown from zero in 2021 to EUR 18 million in 2024 — and we see clear opportunity to replicate this in the Romance language markets.

Customer acquisition cost inflation in direct-to-consumer is the principal risk. Bloom's current 5.2-month payback period has lengthened from 3.8 months in 2022, reflecting both increased competition and broader paid social media cost inflation. We have modelled continued payback elongation to 7 months by exit; the unit economics remain attractive at this level but the trajectory warrants attention.

Brand-driven categories are subject to founder-dependency risk. Sarah Whitmore in particular is closely associated with the brand through content, podcast appearances, and visible founder presence. Sarah has indicated commitment to remain CEO for at least four years post-investment but has expressed interest in stepping back over a longer horizon. We have spent time understanding the brand architecture and believe Bloom has built sufficient institutional brand strength to be sustainable beyond a single founder.

Regulatory risk in women's health is real. Several of Bloom's products make claims around hormonal support and pregnancy wellness that are subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny across European markets. The Company has invested appropriately in regulatory affairs and has a clean track record, but the regulatory environment for nutrition claims is becoming more demanding.

Bloom is a high-quality premium consumer brand in a structurally growing women's health category with strong unit economics and a clear international expansion runway. The entry multiple is full but justified. We recommend approval.

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.

The multiple appears full but reflects Bloom's growth profile (47% revenue CAGR over the past three years), premium positioning, and the strategic optionality created by a well-defined and proven brand platform.

sentences.text: The Company was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists.

occurrences.extract: We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.
COMPANY OVERVIEW

Bloom was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists. The Company operates in the premium women's health and nutrition category, offering a focused range of evidence-based supplement products targeting four primary use cases: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

Bloom operates with a small but capable team of 67 people, headquartered in London with a 12-person team in Berlin focused on the DACH market. The Company has a clinical advisory board of seven specialists across endocrinology, nutrition, and women's health, which contributes to both product development and to the brand's clinical credibility.

Trailing twelve months revenue is EUR 64 million, up from EUR 19 million in 2022 — representing a 47% compound annual growth rate. The recent twelve-month period has shown some deceleration to 31% year-on-year growth as the Company has scaled, but absolute growth remains strong and the unit economics have continued to improve.

Bloom has built a defensible position in a category where most competitors are either single-product brands (limiting customer lifetime value) or insufficiently differentiated. The Company's clinical advisory board, in-house formulation capability, and disciplined product development cadence (typically two new product launches per year) create meaningful competitive moats.

Regulatory risk in women's health is real. Several of Bloom's products make claims around hormonal support and pregnancy wellness that are subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny across European markets. The Company has invested appropriately in regulatory affairs and has a clean track record, but the regulatory environment for nutrition claims is becoming more demanding.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Caraway — Proposed acquisition of Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.

The multiple appears full but reflects Bloom's growth profile (47% revenue CAGR over the past three years), premium positioning, and the strategic optionality created by a well-defined and proven brand platform.

Bloom was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists. The Company operates in the premium women's health and nutrition category, offering a focused range of evidence-based supplement products targeting four primary use cases: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

The product range comprises 24 SKUs, all formulated in-house, manufactured under contract by GMP-certified European facilities, and sold direct-to-consumer through Bloom's own website and Amazon, alongside a select wholesale presence in premium retailers including Selfridges, Le Bon Marché, KaDeWe, and Sephora.

Bloom operates with a small but capable team of 67 people, headquartered in London with a 12-person team in Berlin focused on the DACH market. The Company has a clinical advisory board of seven specialists across endocrinology, nutrition, and women's health, which contributes to both product development and to the brand's clinical credibility.

Premium women's health is a structurally attractive emerging category. Women's health has been historically under-served by both mainstream and premium consumer health brands. The category is growing at approximately 14% annually in Europe, with significantly faster growth in dedicated direct-to-consumer brands. Bloom is well-positioned within this category as a clinically-credible, premium-positioned, multi-product brand.

Bloom has built a defensible position in a category where most competitors are either single-product brands (limiting customer lifetime value) or insufficiently differentiated. The Company's clinical advisory board, in-house formulation capability, and disciplined product development cadence (typically two new product launches per year) create meaningful competitive moats.

International expansion runway is significant. Bloom is strong in the UK and increasingly strong in DACH, but underdeveloped in France, Italy, and Spain. The brand has demonstrable cross-border appeal — DACH revenue has grown from zero in 2021 to EUR 18 million in 2024 — and we see clear opportunity to replicate this in the Romance language markets.

Customer acquisition cost inflation in direct-to-consumer is the principal risk. Bloom's current 5.2-month payback period has lengthened from 3.8 months in 2022, reflecting both increased competition and broader paid social media cost inflation. We have modelled continued payback elongation to 7 months by exit; the unit economics remain attractive at this level but the trajectory warrants attention.

Brand-driven categories are subject to founder-dependency risk. Sarah Whitmore in particular is closely associated with the brand through content, podcast appearances, and visible founder presence. Sarah has indicated commitment to remain CEO for at least four years post-investment but has expressed interest in stepping back over a longer horizon. We have spent time understanding the brand architecture and believe Bloom has built sufficient institutional brand strength to be sustainable beyond a single founder.

Regulatory risk in women's health is real. Several of Bloom's products make claims around hormonal support and pregnancy wellness that are subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny across European markets. The Company has invested appropriately in regulatory affairs and has a clean track record, but the regulatory environment for nutrition claims is becoming more demanding.

Bloom is a high-quality premium consumer brand in a structurally growing women's health category with strong unit economics and a clear international expansion runway. The entry multiple is full but justified. We recommend approval.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Caraway — Proposed acquisition of Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited

We seek IC approval for an investment of EUR 195 million for a 72% controlling stake in Bloom Nutrition Holdings Limited ("Bloom" or "the Company"), a London-headquartered premium women's nutrition and wellness brand with a multi-channel European presence. The transaction values Bloom at an enterprise value of EUR 310 million, representing 14.8x trailing twelve months EBITDA of EUR 21 million.

The multiple appears full but reflects Bloom's growth profile (47% revenue CAGR over the past three years), premium positioning, and the strategic optionality created by a well-defined and proven brand platform.

Bloom was founded in 2018 by Sarah Whitmore and Dr. Lara Bennett, both Cambridge-trained scientists. The Company operates in the premium women's health and nutrition category, offering a focused range of evidence-based supplement products targeting four primary use cases: hormonal balance, energy and recovery, skin and hair health, and pregnancy and postnatal nutrition.

The product range comprises 24 SKUs, all formulated in-house, manufactured under contract by GMP-certified European facilities, and sold direct-to-consumer through Bloom's own website and Amazon, alongside a select wholesale presence in premium retailers including Selfridges, Le Bon Marché, KaDeWe, and Sephora.

Bloom operates with a small but capable team of 67 people, headquartered in London with a 12-person team in Berlin focused on the DACH market. The Company has a clinical advisory board of seven specialists across endocrinology, nutrition, and women's health, which contributes to both product development and to the brand's clinical credibility.

Premium women's health is a structurally attractive emerging category. Women's health has been historically under-served by both mainstream and premium consumer health brands. The category is growing at approximately 14% annually in Europe, with significantly faster growth in dedicated direct-to-consumer brands. Bloom is well-positioned within this category as a clinically-credible, premium-positioned, multi-product brand.

Bloom has built a defensible position in a category where most competitors are either single-product brands (limiting customer lifetime value) or insufficiently differentiated. The Company's clinical advisory board, in-house formulation capability, and disciplined product development cadence (typically two new product launches per year) create meaningful competitive moats.

International expansion runway is significant. Bloom is strong in the UK and increasingly strong in DACH, but underdeveloped in France, Italy, and Spain. The brand has demonstrable cross-border appeal — DACH revenue has grown from zero in 2021 to EUR 18 million in 2024 — and we see clear opportunity to replicate this in the Romance language markets.

Customer acquisition cost inflation in direct-to-consumer is the principal risk. Bloom's current 5.2-month payback period has lengthened from 3.8 months in 2022, reflecting both increased competition and broader paid social media cost inflation. We have modelled continued payback elongation to 7 months by exit; the unit economics remain attractive at this level but the trajectory warrants attention.

Brand-driven categories are subject to founder-dependency risk. Sarah Whitmore in particular is closely associated with the brand through content, podcast appearances, and visible founder presence. Sarah has indicated commitment to remain CEO for at least four years post-investment but has expressed interest in stepping back over a longer horizon. We have spent time understanding the brand architecture and believe Bloom has built sufficient institutional brand strength to be sustainable beyond a single founder.

Regulatory risk in women's health is real. Several of Bloom's products make claims around hormonal support and pregnancy wellness that are subject to evolving regulatory scrutiny across European markets. The Company has invested appropriately in regulatory affairs and has a clean track record, but the regulatory environment for nutrition claims is becoming more demanding.

Bloom is a high-quality premium consumer brand in a structurally growing women's health category with strong unit economics and a clear international expansion runway. The entry multiple is full but justified. We recommend approval.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The memo lands the essentials cleanly and the thesis hangs together. The unit economics are presented in the right order, the channel mix gives a quick read of the business model, and the risk section is honest rather than decorative - calling out that payback has drifted from 3.8 months to 5.2 months is exactly the kind of disclosure the IC will want to see up front. The founder-dependency flag on Sarah Whitmore is also well placed given how the brand is positioned.

That said, the thesis section is doing too much work in one sentence and glosses the hardest question. We say there is 'a clear international runway in France, Italy, Spain, and selectively in the US over a five-year hold,' but we give the reader nothing on sequencing, local CAC assumptions, or why a UK DTC brand should travel - this is the load-bearing assumption behind getting from EUR 64 million to EUR 195 million and it deserves its own paragraph. Relatedly, the base case jump to 2.9x and 24% IRR is asserted without a bridge; even a two-line walk (growth, margin, exit multiple) would make it defensible. I would also tighten the regulatory risk line, which currently trails off vaguely - name the specific claims regimes we are worried about.

reading.writerFeedback:
The draft lands the core thesis well - the geographic breakdown by metro area is clear, the reversion story is quantified and tied to specific submarkets (London and Amsterdam), and the value creation plan has three distinct pillars that readers can follow. The supply-demand framing on urban last-mile is also tight and avoids the usual boilerplate.

A few things weaken it. The claim that 'Urban last-mile is one of the most structurally supported segments of European commercial real estate' is doing a lot of work without any evidence underneath it - either cite a data point or soften it. The returns paragraph is thin given it is the punchline: we get the IRR, MOIC, hold period, and leverage, but no sense of what share of return comes from reversion versus capex versus yield compression, which matters given you have just told the reader the plan rests on all three. I would also push back on 'benefiting from continued rental growth and modest yield compression' as a stated pillar - underwriting yield compression as a value driver reads as aggressive and should either be removed from the plan or explicitly flagged as a sensitivity. Finally, the EUR 38 million capex programme is mentioned once and never sized against the EUR 612 million entry or explained in terms of what the three assets actually need.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The draft lands the core thesis well - the geographic breakdown by metro area is clear, the reversion story is quantified and tied to specific submarkets (London and Amsterdam), and the value creation plan has three distinct pillars that readers can follow. The supply-demand framing on urban last-mile is also tight and avoids the usual boilerplate.

A few things weaken it. The claim that 'Urban last-mile is one of the most structurally supported segments of European commercial real estate' is doing a lot of work without any evidence underneath it - either cite a data point or soften it. The returns paragraph is thin given it is the punchline: we get the IRR, MOIC, hold period, and leverage, but no sense of what share of return comes from reversion versus capex versus yield compression, which matters given you have just told the reader the plan rests on all three. I would also push back on 'benefiting from continued rental growth and modest yield compression' as a stated pillar - underwriting yield compression as a value driver reads as aggressive and should either be removed from the plan or explicitly flagged as a sensitivity. Finally, the EUR 38 million capex programme is mentioned once and never sized against the EUR 612 million entry or explained in terms of what the three assets actually need.

reading.writerFeedback:
The memo lands the essentials cleanly and the three-pillar thesis is well structured, with the product, market, and team strands each supported by a concrete data point. The ARR trajectory from EUR 28 million to EUR 38 million into a base case of EUR 95 million gives the reader a clear growth arc, and anchoring the opportunity in the 40% legacy-systems statistic is effective.

Where it feels thin is the returns bridge - we jump from the ARR path straight to "2.8x MOIC and 23% gross IRR" with nothing on exit multiple assumptions, margin progression, or leverage. The competitive framing also leans heavily on a single comparator ("significantly higher than the principal Nordic competitor Yardi Nordic") without any sense of market share or switching dynamics, and the M&A leg of the growth plan is asserted rather than explained. I would also want a line or two on key risks and on what the 40% minority looks like in governance terms before this goes out.

sentences.text: We are writing to confirm completion of the transaction with Nordic SaaS Holdings (the "Company"), a Stockholm-headquartered B2B SaaS platform serving the Nordic real estate and property management sector.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Lattice — Initial recommendation, Nordic SaaS Holdings AB

We recommend an investment of EUR 158 million for a 60% controlling stake in Nordic SaaS Holdings AB ("NSH" or "the Company"), a Stockholm-headquartered B2B SaaS platform serving the Nordic real estate and property management sector.

NSH was founded in 2013 by Erik Lindqvist (current CEO) and three co-founders. The Company provides an integrated software platform for residential property managers, covering rent collection, maintenance management, tenant communication, and regulatory reporting. The platform serves over 380 property management companies across Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland, collectively managing more than 240,000 residential units.

COMPANY OVERVIEW

NSH was founded in 2013 by Erik Lindqvist (current CEO) and three co-founders. The Company provides an integrated software platform for residential property managers, covering rent collection, maintenance management, tenant communication, and regulatory reporting. The platform serves over 380 property management companies across Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland, collectively managing more than 240,000 residential units.

The Company employs 142 people, with the majority based at the Stockholm headquarters and smaller offices in Oslo (12 people) and Helsinki (8 people). Annual recurring revenue stands at EUR 38 million as of March 2025, up from EUR 28 million the prior year — representing 36% year-on-year growth.

Trailing twelve months revenue is EUR 34 million, with EBITDA of EUR 7.2 million representing a 21% margin. Gross margin is 76% and the Company is free cash flow positive. Net revenue retention is 118% and gross retention is 96%.
The Company has raised approximately EUR 22 million across two prior funding rounds, with the most recent being a Series B led by Atomico in 2022 that valued NSH at EUR 110 million pre-money.

Third, the founder team is exceptional. Erik Lindqvist is a domain-deep CEO who has rebuilt the product from the ground up over the past four years. The technical leadership has been stable and capable, with the CTO (Pekka Virtanen) having been with the Company since 2015.
EBITDA margin is expected to expand from 21% to 32% over the hold as the Company achieves greater operational scale and as Rule of 40 discipline drives more efficient growth.

Annual recurring revenue at end of April was EUR 35 million, not EUR 38 million as stated in our initial memo. The discrepancy arose from the Company's internal reporting convention, which has historically included committed but not yet activated annual contracts in the headline ARR figure. The cleaned ARR (representing live, billing customer contracts only) is EUR 35 million. Growth on a cleaned basis is 28% year-on-year rather than the 36% previously reported.

This is a meaningful adjustment but does not fundamentally change the investment thesis. The cleaned ARR figure is reflected in our updated returns analysis below. We have agreed with Company management to migrate to the cleaned ARR convention for all future reporting.

The Company employs 167 people as of 28 May, not 142 as stated in our initial memo. The difference reflects (a) the closing of two Norwegian hiring rounds that completed in late April and (b) the inclusion of approximately 18 contractors who function as full-time team members but had been excluded from the headcount provided to us initially.
The Company currently serves 412 property management companies, not 380 as stated in our initial memo. This is a positive update reflecting strong net new logo addition over the past two months.

Confirmatory diligence raised no other material issues. Bain & Company's customer reference work confirmed the strength of the product and the relationship picture. Deloitte's financial diligence confirmed the underlying revenue quality, cash generation, and working capital position. KPMG's tax review identified no items of concern. Slaughter and May's legal diligence identified two minor commercial contract items that have been addressed through specific indemnities in the SPA.

occurrences.extract: We recommend an investment of EUR 158 million for a 60% controlling stake in Nordic SaaS Holdings AB ("NSH" or "the Company"), a Stockholm-headquartered B2B SaaS platform serving the Nordic real estate and property management sector.
COMPANY OVERVIEW

NSH was founded in 2013 by Erik Lindqvist (current CEO) and three co-founders. The Company provides an integrated software platform for residential property managers, covering rent collection, maintenance management, tenant communication, and regulatory reporting. The platform serves over 380 property management companies across Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland, collectively managing more than 240,000 residential units.

The Company employs 142 people, with the majority based at the Stockholm headquarters and smaller offices in Oslo (12 people) and Helsinki (8 people). Annual recurring revenue stands at EUR 38 million as of March 2025, up from EUR 28 million the prior year — representing 36% year-on-year growth.

Trailing twelve months revenue is EUR 34 million, with EBITDA of EUR 7.2 million representing a 21% margin. Gross margin is 76% and the Company is free cash flow positive. Net revenue retention is 118% and gross retention is 96%.
The Company has raised approximately EUR 22 million across two prior funding rounds, with the most recent being a Series B led by Atomico in 2022 that valued NSH at EUR 110 million pre-money.

Third, the founder team is exceptional. Erik Lindqvist is a domain-deep CEO who has rebuilt the product from the ground up over the past four years. The technical leadership has been stable and capable, with the CTO (Pekka Virtanen) having been with the Company since 2015.
EBITDA margin is expected to expand from 21% to 32% over the hold as the Company achieves greater operational scale and as Rule of 40 discipline drives more efficient growth.

Annual recurring revenue at end of April was EUR 35 million, not EUR 38 million as stated in our initial memo. The discrepancy arose from the Company's internal reporting convention, which has historically included committed but not yet activated annual contracts in the headline ARR figure. The cleaned ARR (representing live, billing customer contracts only) is EUR 35 million. Growth on a cleaned basis is 28% year-on-year rather than the 36% previously reported.

This is a meaningful adjustment but does not fundamentally change the investment thesis. The cleaned ARR figure is reflected in our updated returns analysis below. We have agreed with Company management to migrate to the cleaned ARR convention for all future reporting.

The Company employs 167 people as of 28 May, not 142 as stated in our initial memo. The difference reflects (a) the closing of two Norwegian hiring rounds that completed in late April and (b) the inclusion of approximately 18 contractors who function as full-time team members but had been excluded from the headcount provided to us initially.
The Company currently serves 412 property management companies, not 380 as stated in our initial memo. This is a positive update reflecting strong net new logo addition over the past two months.

Confirmatory diligence raised no other material issues. Bain & Company's customer reference work confirmed the strength of the product and the relationship picture. Deloitte's financial diligence confirmed the underlying revenue quality, cash generation, and working capital position. KPMG's tax review identified no items of concern. Slaughter and May's legal diligence identified two minor commercial contract items that have been addressed through specific indemnities in the SPA.

occurrences.extract: Subject:   Project Lattice — Initial recommendation, Nordic SaaS Holdings AB

We recommend an investment of EUR 158 million for a 60% controlling stake in Nordic SaaS Holdings AB ("NSH" or "the Company"), a Stockholm-headquartered B2B SaaS platform serving the Nordic real estate and property management sector.

First, the product is genuinely market-leading. Independent customer research conducted as part of diligence rated NSH significantly higher than the principal Nordic competitor (Yardi Nordic) on usability, feature completeness, and customer support. NPS scores are in the high 60s, exceptional for B2B software.

Second, the Nordic property management technology market remains structurally underpenetrated. Approximately 40% of Nordic property management companies still use legacy systems or spreadsheets. NSH has a clear runway to continue penetrating this addressable market.

The principal risks are (a) competitive response from Yardi or other larger international software platforms entering the Nordic market more aggressively, (b) consolidation of property management companies themselves, which could reduce the addressable customer base, and (c) execution risk in the planned adjacent expansion into commercial property management, where NSH has limited current presence.
NSH is a high-quality Nordic vertical SaaS asset with strong unit economics, exceptional product strength, and a clear growth runway. We recommend approval.

To:        Investment Committee
From:      Tech Team — Sarah Klein (Member of Management), Marco Bianchi (Senior Vice President)
Subject:   Project Lattice — Initial recommendation, Nordic SaaS Holdings AB
RECOMMENDATION

We recommend an investment of EUR 158 million for a 60% controlling stake in Nordic SaaS Holdings AB ("NSH" or "the Company"), a Stockholm-headquartered B2B SaaS platform serving the Nordic real estate and property management sector.
COMPANY OVERVIEW

NSH was founded in 2013 by Erik Lindqvist (current CEO) and three co-founders. The Company provides an integrated software platform for residential property managers, covering rent collection, maintenance management, tenant communication, and regulatory reporting. The platform serves over 380 property management companies across Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland, collectively managing more than 240,000 residential units.

The Company employs 142 people, with the majority based at the Stockholm headquarters and smaller offices in Oslo (12 people) and Helsinki (8 people). Annual recurring revenue stands at EUR 38 million as of March 2025, up from EUR 28 million the prior year — representing 36% year-on-year growth.

Trailing twelve months revenue is EUR 34 million, with EBITDA of EUR 7.2 million representing a 21% margin. Gross margin is 76% and the Company is free cash flow positive. Net revenue retention is 118% and gross retention is 96%.
The Company has raised approximately EUR 22 million across two prior funding rounds, with the most recent being a Series B led by Atomico in 2022 that valued NSH at EUR 110 million pre-money.
INVESTMENT THESIS

First, the product is genuinely market-leading. Independent customer research conducted as part of diligence rated NSH significantly higher than the principal Nordic competitor (Yardi Nordic) on usability, feature completeness, and customer support. NPS scores are in the high 60s, exceptional for B2B software.

Second, the Nordic property management technology market remains structurally underpenetrated. Approximately 40% of Nordic property management companies still use legacy systems or spreadsheets. NSH has a clear runway to continue penetrating this addressable market.

Third, the founder team is exceptional. Erik Lindqvist is a domain-deep CEO who has rebuilt the product from the ground up over the past four years. The technical leadership has been stable and capable, with the CTO (Pekka Virtanen) having been with the Company since 2015.

Our base case envisages ARR growth from EUR 38 million today to approximately EUR 95 million over a five-year hold. This is supported by continued strong organic growth (we underwrite 22% ARR CAGR over the hold period), modest expansion into adjacent verticals (commercial property management), and selective add-on M&A.
EBITDA margin is expected to expand from 21% to 32% over the hold as the Company achieves greater operational scale and as Rule of 40 discipline drives more efficient growth.
The base case generates a 2.8x MOIC and 23% IRR.

The principal risks are (a) competitive response from Yardi or other larger international software platforms entering the Nordic market more aggressively, (b) consolidation of property management companies themselves, which could reduce the addressable customer base, and (c) execution risk in the planned adjacent expansion into commercial property management, where NSH has limited current presence.
NSH is a high-quality Nordic vertical SaaS asset with strong unit economics, exceptional product strength, and a clear growth runway. We recommend approval.
POST-SIGNING CONFIRMATORY DILIGENCE — STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL
To:        Investment Committee
From:      Tech Team — Sarah Klein (Member of Management), Marco Bianchi (Senior Vice President)
Date:      28 May 2025
Subject:   Project Lattice — Updated findings from confirmatory diligence, Nordic SaaS Holdings AB

This memo provides an update to the Investment Committee following completion of confirmatory diligence on NSH. Two findings warrant Committee attention as they materially update the picture set out in the initial recommendation of 15 April.

Annual recurring revenue at end of April was EUR 35 million, not EUR 38 million as stated in our initial memo. The discrepancy arose from the Company's internal reporting convention, which has historically included committed but not yet activated annual contracts in the headline ARR figure. The cleaned ARR (representing live, billing customer contracts only) is EUR 35 million. Growth on a cleaned basis is 28% year-on-year rather than the 36% previously reported.

This is a meaningful adjustment but does not fundamentally change the investment thesis. The cleaned ARR figure is reflected in our updated returns analysis below. We have agreed with Company management to migrate to the cleaned ARR convention for all future reporting.
UPDATED EMPLOYEE COUNT

The Company employs 167 people as of 28 May, not 142 as stated in our initial memo. The difference reflects (a) the closing of two Norwegian hiring rounds that completed in late April and (b) the inclusion of approximately 18 contractors who function as full-time team members but had been excluded from the headcount provided to us initially.

This higher headcount has implications for our operating leverage assumptions. We have updated our base case to reflect the higher current cost base, partially offset by reduced incremental hiring in the early years of our ownership.
UPDATED CUSTOMER COUNT
The Company currently serves 412 property management companies, not 380 as stated in our initial memo. This is a positive update reflecting strong net new logo addition over the past two months.

The combined effect of the above updates is a modest reduction in our underwritten returns. Our updated base case generates a 2.6x MOIC and 21% IRR over the five-year hold, compared with the 2.8x / 23% in our initial recommendation. The investment remains attractive and we are not recommending changes to the transaction structure or pricing.

Confirmatory diligence raised no other material issues. Bain & Company's customer reference work confirmed the strength of the product and the relationship picture. Deloitte's financial diligence confirmed the underlying revenue quality, cash generation, and working capital position. KPMG's tax review identified no items of concern. Slaughter and May's legal diligence identified two minor commercial contract items that have been addressed through specific indemnities in the SPA.
We continue to recommend completion of the transaction on the terms set out in the original recommendation, subject to acknowledgment of the updated financial and operational figures above.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The memo lands the essentials cleanly and the three-pillar thesis is well structured, with the product, market, and team strands each supported by a concrete data point. The ARR trajectory from EUR 28 million to EUR 38 million into a base case of EUR 95 million gives the reader a clear growth arc, and anchoring the opportunity in the 40% legacy-systems statistic is effective.

Where it feels thin is the returns bridge - we jump from the ARR path straight to "2.8x MOIC and 23% gross IRR" with nothing on exit multiple assumptions, margin progression, or leverage. The competitive framing also leans heavily on a single comparator ("significantly higher than the principal Nordic competitor Yardi Nordic") without any sense of market share or switching dynamics, and the M&A leg of the growth plan is asserted rather than explained. I would also want a line or two on key risks and on what the 40% minority looks like in governance terms before this goes out.

reading.writerFeedback:
The draft reads clearly and the structure works well - headline Fund metrics up front, NorTech as the realisation story, then a disciplined walk through the remaining portfolio before ESG and the forward look. The Eltex passage is the strongest in the draft because the backlog growth from EUR 285 million to EUR 480 million does real work alongside the revenue and EBITDA figures, and the Continental Plastics paragraph is handled honestly, pairing the miss with the specific operational response and the 12-month timeline slip rather than burying it.

Where it is weaker is in the two problem companies, which could use one more line each on investor implications. On Continental Plastics we are told the realisation timeline has lengthened "by approximately 12 months" but not what that means for hold period or expected MOIC at exit, and on Drift Logistics the margin compression from 14 to 12% is stated without any view on whether this is cyclical or structural, or what management is doing about it. The ESG paragraph is also a little mechanical and would benefit from a sentence tying the 34% figure and the SBTi progress back to something that matters commercially or to LPs, rather than reading as a standalone scorecard. One small structural point: Helvetia and Lumen are dispatched in half a sentence each, which is fine given they are new, but consider whether grouping them explicitly as "recent acquisitions, both on plan" would read more cleanly than the current run-on.

fixtures.writerFeedback:
The draft reads clearly and the structure works well - headline Fund metrics up front, NorTech as the realisation story, then a disciplined walk through the remaining portfolio before ESG and the forward look. The Eltex passage is the strongest in the draft because the backlog growth from EUR 285 million to EUR 480 million does real work alongside the revenue and EBITDA figures, and the Continental Plastics paragraph is handled honestly, pairing the miss with the specific operational response and the 12-month timeline slip rather than burying it.

Where it is weaker is in the two problem companies, which could use one more line each on investor implications. On Continental Plastics we are told the realisation timeline has lengthened "by approximately 12 months" but not what that means for hold period or expected MOIC at exit, and on Drift Logistics the margin compression from 14 to 12% is stated without any view on whether this is cyclical or structural, or what management is doing about it. The ESG paragraph is also a little mechanical and would benefit from a sentence tying the 34% figure and the SBTi progress back to something that matters commercially or to LPs, rather than reading as a standalone scorecard. One small structural point: Helvetia and Lumen are dispatched in half a sentence each, which is fine given they are new, but consider whether grouping them explicitly as "recent acquisitions, both on plan" would read more cleanly than the current run-on.

reading.writerFeedback:
The announcement reads well overall and lands the key proof points quickly - hard cap, step-up from Fund IV, speed of raise, and oversubscription all come through in the first few lines. The LP composition detail is also a strength, particularly the specifics around "three of the largest US public pension funds, two Asian sovereign wealth funds" and the 96% re-up rate, which give the piece credibility beyond the headline number.

Where it feels thinner is the back half. The strategy paragraph is generic - "advanced manufacturing, energy transition, and specialty chemicals" could sit in almost any European industrials announcement, and there is nothing on what differentiates Meridian's angle or why these sectors now. The closing line that "Our investment team has been preparing Fund V's pipeline for many months" is soft and does not really say anything; I would either cut it or replace it with something concrete about pipeline visibility or a signalled first deal. One other thing worth a look: the EUR 1.2 billion of excess demand sits oddly next to the 11-month timeline without any comment on why the hard cap was held, and a line on LP discipline there would strengthen the message rather than leave the reader to infer it.
